articles.title: 40 years after the Anti-Drug Abuse Act, punishment is law and treatment is lacking
articles.summary: The reality 40 years later is that Congress made the drug penalties permanent law, while drug treatment was left to be determined during annual budget fights.
articles.body:
When the Boston Celtics drafted Len Bias second overall on June 17, 1986, he told reporters, “ My dream has come true. ” Two days later, he died after his cocaine use triggered a fatal cardiac event. He was 22.

In response to the national alarm following Bias’s death, on Oct. 27, 1986, President Ronald Reagan signed the Anti-Drug Abuse Act and promised it was “not intended as a means of filling our jails with drug users.” The country’s job, he said, was to reach people who use drugs and help them quit.

In that instance, Congress acted with a purpose Americans across the political spectrum shared: reduce drug use and save lives. Despite that good intention, the reality 40 years later is that Congress made the drug penalties permanent law, while drug treatment was left to be determined during annual budget fights. That imbalance is the law’s most lasting legacy.

In 1986, Congress wrote the penalties quickly. Eric Sterling, the House Judiciary Committee counsel who worked on the bill, later recalled that the mandatory minimums were added in the final days before the August recess, as members headed home to campaign. The drug quantities that triggered them received no hearings.

Five grams of crack cocaine, about the weight of a nickel, drew the same five-year minimum as 500 grams of powder, which weighs more than a pound. Crack cocaine produces a faster, more intense high when smoked than powder does when snorted, but it is not 100 times more powerful. The U.S. Sentencing Commission later found nothing in the legislative record explaining that 100 to 1 ratio. More than two decades after his death, a House committee acknowledged that Bias died from powder cocaine, not crack.

The costs fell unevenly and lasted for decades. In 1993, 88 percent of people convicted of federal crack trafficking offenses were Black. By 2011, the federal prison population had tripled in 20 years , and the Sentencing Commission named mandatory minimums as one cause. Congress has spent decades narrowing the crack-powder gap, and an 18 to 1 ratio is still federal law.

The law’s title also promised to “ expand Federal support for drug abuse treatment and rehabilitation efforts ,” but that promise needed money every year. In January 1987, 10 weeks after the signing, the administration’s budget requested no new money for drug treatment services, according to members of the House narcotics committee. Rep. Benjamin Gilman (R-N.Y.), the committee’s senior Republican, called the cuts “appalling.”

Treatment has been the weaker half ever since. Much of the federal money behind treatment and overdose response is still renewed one year at a time. In 2025, 84 percent of the 47.2 million people who needed substance use treatment did not receive it, according to the federal government’s own survey.

The distance between permanent punishment and temporary care is widest and most deadly following incarceration. A study of people released from North Carolina prisons found that in their first two weeks home, they died of opioid overdoses at 40 times the rate of the state’s general population.

Congress knows how to make treatment permanent. In 2024, it made permanent Medicaid’s coverage of medications for opioid use disorder. Federal law still generally bars Medicaid from paying for care during incarceration, so states have relied on waivers to start treatment before release. In September, however, federal officials cut the maximum pre-release window for future adult waivers from 90 days to 60. No vote was required.

The bipartisan Reentry Act would address this by letting every state cover the last 30 days before release without a waiver; a floor no agency could shrink. Congress should address the deadliest gap in treatment by including the Reentry Act in the year-end spending package before current funding expires Dec. 11 . Congress should also keep the federal grants that pay for addiction treatment intact rather than fold them into a single block grant , as the president’s budget proposes.

In 1986, Congress acted on a young man’s untimely death with a speed it could not match when the consequences of its choices became clear. Forty years later, the penalties remain certain, while access to treatment remains questionable. It’s time for lawmakers to change that.

Libby Jones is associate vice president of the Overdose Prevention Initiative at the Global Health Advocacy Incubator. Regina LaBelle is a professor and director of Georgetown University’s Master of Addiction Policy and Practice program. She served in the White House Office of National Drug Control Policy in both the Biden and Obama administrations.

articles.title: Ty Cobb predicts Trump will likely skip deposition, dismiss BBC lawsuit
articles.summary: Former White House attorney Ty Cobb said President Trump would likely skip a mandated deposition or walk out in the middle, which he predicted would lead to the eventual dismissal of the president’s lawsuit against the BBC. Cobb joined CNN’s Erin Burnett on Thursday night after a judge said Trump must sit for a deposition…
articles.body:
Former White House attorney Ty Cobb said President Trump would likely skip a mandated deposition or walk out in the middle, which he predicted would lead to the eventual dismissal of the president’s lawsuit against the BBC.

Cobb joined CNN’s Erin Burnett on Thursday night after a judge said Trump must sit for a deposition in his $10 billion suit against the British broadcaster. Cobb said Trump would likely skip the deposition, as he has done once before, and the judge would throw out the case.

“They’re trying to get his deposition, which they’re entitled to, or the case will be dismissed,” Cobb said.

Trump sued the BBC for defaming him in a documentary in which parts of his speech on Jan. 6, 2021, were spliced together to make it seem that he was calling for violence. The BBC acknowledged the error and brought in new leadership, but it is denying the claim that its actions amounted to defamation.

Cobb said the lawsuit was backfiring, highlighting that unlike other media outlets that Trump has sued for what the former White House lawyer called “stories that he didn’t like” but were truthful, the BBC is refusing to settle the case. Trump was set to be deposed earlier this month but canceled due to a “matter of national importance.” He held a campaign rally in Georgia later that day.

“Trump has dragged it out. He’s the plaintiff in the case. He’s the one that invented these claims,” Cobb said, adding that Trump hoped the BBC would cave and pay the president in a settlement, which did not happen.

U.S. Magistrate Judge Enjoliqué Lett said Trump must sit for a deposition by Dec. 11 or face the potential dismissal of the case. He ruled that the deposition would be recorded on video but not released to the public.

“Trump will never sit for it. He’s likely to refuse to go,” Cobb said. “If he does go, he’ll walk out in the middle and the case will ultimately get dismissed unless that the plaintiffs are entitled to and receive his full testimony.”

articles.title: Cook Political Report shifts 19 House seats in Democrats’ favor
articles.summary: Nonpartisan election forecaster Cook Political Report has shifted 19 House seats in Democrats’ direction less than two weeks before the midterm elections, according to its latest report published Friday. The shift includes six Republicans whose races were previously noted as “toss-ups” and have now been changed to “Lean Democrat”: Reps. Juan Ciscomani (Ariz.), Gabe Evans (Colo.), Jen…
articles.body:
Nonpartisan election forecaster Cook Political Report has shifted 19 House seats in Democrats’ direction less than two weeks before the midterm elections, according to its latest report published Friday.

The shift includes six Republicans whose races were previously noted as “toss-ups” and have now been changed to “Lean Democrat”: Reps. Juan Ciscomani (Ariz.), Gabe Evans (Colo.), Jen Kiggans (Va.) and Derrick Van Orden (Wis.).

“Following this latest round of ratings changes, Democrats now are favored outright in the 218 seats they need to win control of the House,” Cook Political Report’s U.S. House editor Erin Covey wrote in the report. “Republicans, meanwhile, are favored in 198 seats, rated Solid, Likely, or Lean Republican. That leaves 17 races rated as pure Toss Ups.”

Two open seats — in Kentucky’s 6th District and Texas’s 35th District — have been moved from “Lean Republican” to “toss-up,” according to Cook’s predictions. In Kentucky’s 6th District, Democrat Zach Dembo is facing Republican Ralph Alvarado. In Texas’s 35th District, Democrat Johnny Garcia is going up against Republican Carlos De La Cruz.

Per Cook’s analysis, the “likeliest outcome” is “Democrats flipping between 12 and 22 seats.” According to the projections, Democrats will hold anywhere between 227 to 237 seats next year, while Republicans are projected to hold between 198 and 208 seats.

Cook’s analysis comes as President Trump’s approval ratings hit new lows in the latest polls from The New York Times/Siena University and CNN in the final stretch of the upcoming midterm elections. The Times reported Tuesday that the president’s 36 percent approval was a record low for all Times/Siena polls.

Trump’s approval rating in the CNN poll stood at 32 percent, also a historic low as reported by the outlet Tuesday , with voters expressing broad dissatisfaction with both the economy and the state of the country.

articles.title: Wall Street Journal editorial board hits Marshall for backing Social Security tax increase
articles.summary: The Wall Street Journal editorial board on Thursday took GOP Sen. Roger Marshall (Kan.) to task for backing an elimination of the cap on income subject to Social Security taxes. Marshall, the Journal editorial board wrote, is in “favor of what would be one of the largest peacetime tax increases in recent decades” by advocating…
articles.body:
The Wall Street Journal editorial board on Thursday took GOP Sen. Roger Marshall (Kan.) to task for backing an elimination of the cap on income subject to Social Security taxes.

Marshall, the Journal editorial board wrote , is in “favor of what would be one of the largest peacetime tax increases in recent decades” by advocating for the federal government to scrap the cap.

The maximum amount of yearly earnings on which taxpayers must hand over a portion of their paycheck to fund Social Security is $184,500. The Social Security Administration raises the cap on an annual basis to “keep pace with increases in average wages,” according to its website .

During a debate Wednesday against Adam Hamilton, his Democratic opponent in the Senate race in Kansas, Marshall said he supports eliminating the cap “altogether.” The Kansas Republican deflected on raising the retirement age, saying lawmakers could “exhaust” other options first.

“It will take Republicans and Democrats working together,” Marshall said. “There’s no easy answer, because we have more people retiring than entering the workforce.”

Hamilton, a Methodist pastor, said he supported raising the cap instead of “taking it away entirely.” The Democratic nominee said he would “look at” raising the retirement age but did not commit to supporting such a move.

The Journal editorial board blasted the proposed elimination of the cap as a “bad idea,” saying Marshall effectively supports a larger tax increase than his Democratic opponent.

“Raising or eliminating that cap has become Democrats’ go-to Social Security plan because it looks like a way to tax the rich to give to the elderly poor,” the editorial board wrote. “Never mind that under the most optimistic assumptions, eliminating the cap wouldn’t come close to filling the entitlement’s funding gap.”

The board added, “Why vote for Republicans if all you’ll get is left-wing, tax-and-spend economic policies masquerading as right-wing populism?”

Trump administration officials warned earlier this year that Social Security’s Old-Age and Survivors Insurance Trust Fund will only be able to cover 78 percent of benefits starting in the early 2030s.

That has spurred lawmakers to propose multiple ideas for how to address the impending funding shortfall , including an increase or elimination of the payroll cap and the federal government investing in the stock market to increase revenue for the program.

The Journal editorial board noted that reforming payroll taxes “may be part of a Social Security fix” down the road.

“But adjustments to the retirement age, changes to cost-of-living adjustments, and means-testing benefits all need to be on the table, too,” the board argued.

articles.title: Trump’s border chief defends planned wall in Texas’ Big Bend despite court-ordered pause
articles.summary: The Trump administration’s top border official defended plans to build a wall and other infrastructure in Texas' Big Bend region despite mounting opposition.
articles.body: BLAINE, Wash. — The Trump administration’s top border official defended plans to build a wall and other infrastructure in Texas' Big Bend region despite mounting opposition against the project and a court-ordered pause on construction, saying his goal of fortifying the country's borders was “non-negotiable.” In an exclusive interview with The Associated Press, Customs and Border Protection Commissioner Rodney Scott argued that the $46 billion wall project was justified despite a bipartisan coalition of landowners, local businesses and environmentalists who view it as a waste of taxpayer money that could be destructive to a region with historically low migrant crossings. “Our number one goal right out the gate is we have to know who and what is coming into the United States,” Scott said on Thursday. If the Big Bend region were left without a wall or other border infrastructure while other areas along the border get those fortifications, he said, “I am 100% convinced it will be completely overrun and destroyed.” The fight over Big Bend has become a major test for how far the Republican administration is willing to go for the border wall, President Donald Trump's signature infrastructure project. Scott, a former Border Patrol agent, was tapped by Trump to complete it. His agency is responsible for executing a plan funded last summer by Republicans in Congress to line the roughly 2,000-mile (3,200-kilometer) border with Mexico with a mixture of 30-foot-tall (9-meter-tall) steel walls, vehicle barriers, new roads and surveillance technology to prevent illegal immigration and smuggling. The Trump administration says it is building about 12 miles (19 kilometers) a week. Scott, who gets daily progress updates, said it will be complete by the end of Trump's second term. The primary border wall — some areas also get a secondary layer — will be done by the end of December 2027. “We’re actually ahead of schedule,” Scott said. Big Bend is a test for the Trump administration's plans for the wall The wall plan has run into resistance in places like Big Bend. The Trump administration suffered a major setback earlier this month when a judge ordered a pause on border wall construction in the region, citing what could be a likelihood that plaintiffs “will suffer serious, irreparable harm without an injunction.” The administration has asked the Supreme Court to lift the order. The ruling included any construction in Big Bend National Park, an area that has seen a loud bipartisan outcry, including from some Republican lawmakers. After bulldozers were spotted in the park tearing up ground in August, Scott ordered a pause on all construction-related activity there while he went to talk to people in the region. He said the agency is making other outreach to locals to discuss how to build projects so they don’t mar the park. “We’re talking through and figuring out what is the right solution for that area,” he said. Scott said he can’t get into specific details on what the agency’s plans are for the park due to the numerous ongoing lawsuits, but he reiterated that the project won't include tall steel walls. He also said that the agency’s stated goal of protecting the country and knowing what’s coming in and going out is “non-negotiable.” He said the region's formidable natural barriers were not enough to prevent people from entering the country illegally through other more navigable points. And he expressed concern that cartels that control smuggling from Mexico into the U.S. would exploit any opening. CBP has come under fire for immigration enforcement tactics Scott leads an agency of 67,000 employees responsible for controlling who and what comes into the country through official border crossings like airports or seaports and stopping illegal smuggling and migration outside those official border crossing points. The agency came under heavy scrutiny last year when its officers were sent into cities deep inside the country to help carry out Trump's immigration crackdown alongside Immigration and Customs Enforcement. As protests against an operation rocked Minneapolis, a Border Patrol officer and a CBP officer both fired shots in an encounter that killed a U.S. citizen, Alex Pretti. The shooting eventually prompted the Trump administration to wind down high-profile city-based crackdowns. A CBP officer who was the face of the missions, Gregory Bovino, who led a helicopter raid at a large apartment building and used chemical agents to confront demonstrators, retired earlier this year. Scott said while CBP still helps ICE, it's now less involved in immigration enforcement far from the country's borders because ICE has since hired more officers to its ranks. Scott wouldn't comment on the investigation into the Pretti killing, saying that it was being handled by the FBI and was ongoing. And when asked about Bovino's tactics, he said the officer didn't report to him during the operations. Scott spoke to the AP just outside the border with Canada, where he met with border security representatives from other countries to share information about threats and trends. During his trip, he visited an operations center where he said Canadian and American law enforcement work together. That border has far fewer threats than the U.S. border with Mexico. Scott said cartels in Mexico are increasingly sending drones into the United States to move contraband and keep tabs on Border Patrol agents. In Mexico, the cartels have been using drones to attack each other or Mexican law enforcement. The Department of Homeland Security, which includes CBP, recently announced temporary flight restrictions targeting unauthorized drone activity in a zone extending a mile (1.6 kilometers) north of the U.S.-Mexico border as a way to counter cartels. “We want to make sure," Scott said, “that threat does not come into the United States.”

articles.title: Jackson again publicly breaks with Supreme Court as justices side with GOP in last-minute voter ID fight
articles.summary: Ketanji Brown Jackson publicly dissented as the Supreme Court let New Hampshire block student ID cards as ballot identification for midterm elections.
articles.body: Supreme Court Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson was the lone public dissenter in a Thursday decision allowing New Hampshire to block the use of student ID cards in the upcoming midterm elections. Other justices on the court cited the longstanding precedent "that lower federal courts should ordinarily not alter the election rules on the eve of an election," and said that lower courts failed to argue that the specific case in New Hampshire warranted an exception to the tradition. Jackson, however, argued the proximity to an election should not get in the way of properly applying the law. "I respectfully dissent because — even, and perhaps especially, when an election is looming — I would not disturb a clearly justifiable federal-court order issued to ensure that the public receives accurate information about a State’s electoral processes," she wrote. FEDERAL JUDGE BLOCKS INDIANA BAN ON STUDENT ID FOR VOTING The underlying dispute stems from a law signed in April that went into effect in June, striking student ID cards from the list of forms of identification that election officials can accept when an individual requests a ballot. A voting rights group sued New Hampshire on the grounds that the law illegally discriminated against young voters by making it more difficult for them to vote. New Hampshire Secretary of State David Scanlan then issued guidance saying that student IDs could not be used to establish voter identity, even as supporting evidence under the state's alternative verification procedures. A district judge blocked that portion of the guidance, arguing that it went beyond the scope of the law itself, which only removed student IDs from the list of expressly accepted forms of identification. Among the supporters of the guidance was the Republican National Committee. DEMS HAND GOP FRESH MIDTERM WEAPON BY OPPOSING WIDELY USED VOTER ID While Jackson was the lone public dissenter, it is possible that other justices dissented as well, but opted not to be named on the court order. During her roughly four years on the Supreme Court, Jackson has broken from the rest of her colleagues in areas such as campaign finance, immigration and congressional map litigation. In 2023, she was the lone dissenter in an 8-1 ruling allowing a concrete company to sue striking union workers. She also stood alone in a May 2026 decision involving federal prisoners seeking to challenge their convictions through compassionate release. TRUMP SCORES SUPREME COURT WIN IN ELECTION INTEGRITY FIGHT AS STATES GAIN NEW VOTER ROLL TOOL New Hampshire is holding a handful of close races on Election Day, putting some weight behind the court’s decision. Fox News’ power rankings rate the state’s Senate race as leans Democratic, meaning that liberals have a slight advantage in a race that could decide control of Congress. The state’s governor’s race, meanwhile, is rated as likely going to the GOP. College students typically favor the Democratic Party, though it is unclear how many voters will be affected by the court ruling, as students who previously relied on their student IDs will now need another accepted form of identification. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Some Democrats, however, believe allowing voters to use student IDs would be a good thing. Texas Democratic Senate nominee James Talarico, for instance, has pushed for such a thing in his state.

articles.title: Manchin: Collins should leave GOP, become an independent
articles.summary: Former Sen. Joe Manchin (I-W.Va.) suggested this week that Maine Sen. Susan Collins (R) should leave the Republican Party to become an independent. Manchin, who made the switch from the Democratic Party to become an independent in 2024, has repeatedly pushed for more lawmakers to break away from the two-party system. The former senator told…
articles.body:
Former Sen. Joe Manchin (I-W.Va.) suggested this week that Maine Sen. Susan Collins (R) should leave the Republican Party to become an independent.

Manchin, who made the switch from the Democratic Party to become an independent in 2024, has repeatedly pushed for more lawmakers to break away from the two-party system.

The former senator told Semafor after joining the Maine incumbent on the campaign trail this week that Collins “is independent” but that she “has to come to that conclusion” first.

“She’s as independent as any Republican is up there,” Manchin told the outlet. “But the bottom line is, she has to make that decision.”

The Hill has reached out to the Maine senator’s campaign for comment.

Manchin visited a New Balance shoe factory in southwestern Maine for a campaign stop with Collins this week, after endorsing her reelection bid in September.

The senator has built a reputation in Congress as a moderate Republican, breaking with her party on key votes like an April Iran war powers resolution .

She also voted to convict President Trump in his second impeachment trial in 2021 and opposed repealing the Affordable Care Act in 2017.

Collins is seeking a sixth term in the Senate in a closely watched reelection race in the Pine Tree State against Democratic nominee Troy Jackson.

Cook Political Report, a nonpartisan election handicapper, rates the race as a “toss up.” A Fox News poll released Thursday showed the two candidates tied at 49 percent. Recent polls from Suffolk University and Marist University have shown Jackson posting moderate leads over the incumbent senator that fall within the surveys’ margins of error.

Manchin also told Semafor that he is working with the Independent Leadership Council , which he co-founded in July, to support candidates running in Montana, Idaho and Nebraska. The group aims to elect more independent leaders to Congress.

articles.title: White House says Melania Trump brokers truce for Ukraine city 'on brink of disaster'
articles.summary: Ukraine and Russia confirm the truce in Russian-occupied Oleshky, where residents have had to eat garden weeds to survive.
articles.body:
US First Lady Melania Trump has "successfully secured" a ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine in the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky, the White House has said.

It said the truce in the "front-line war city on the brink of disaster" without medicine, food and clean water would begin on 29 October.

Ukraine and Russia confirmed the deal was agreed to evacuate residents and deliver aid. Moscow said its forces would stop firing at 04:00 (02:00 GMT) on 27 October.

Oleshky was seized by Russia during the first days of its full-scale invasion in February 2022. Trapped between Ukrainian positions across the Dnipro River and Russian forces to the east, residents have recently resorted to eating garden weeds to survive.

The White House statement said Melania Trump and one of her representatives had worked "directly with Russian and Ukrainian leadership to define the terms of the localised ceasefire".

"Non-military, civilian leaders from both countries will work together to visit Oleshky residents in their homes and determine the level of assistance they require," she is quoted as saying.

"Residents who wish to evacuate will receive co-ordinated support and transportation to their preferred destination. I anticipate some will want to go to Russia, and some to Ukraine."

Melania Trump added that Oleshky residents "have limited electricity, live amid mined roads, and endure regular military attacks" and that "without my intervention, the possibility to bring humanitarian aid into the city and to evacuate the elderly would be impossible".

The statement did not say how long the ceasefire would be in place for.

Davyd Arakhamia, a Ukrainian MP who heads President Volodymyr Zelensky's party in parliament, later said "an operation to unblock the settlement of Oleshky and its surroundings will begin in the near future".

"To achieve this goal, a ceasefire will be achieved in the near future, as announced by the First Lady of the United States, Melania Trump," he said. No date or time has been announced by Kyiv yet.

In Russia, President Vladimir Putin's spokesman confirmed that, "those who wish to do so will be able to leave this settlement".

Last month, some of the remaining Oleshky residents told the BBC harrowing accounts of how they were surviving in the city that was being constantly shelled and cut off from food and water.

They said that children remaining in wider Oleshky were suffering from malnutrition, a lack of medical services and were "degrading" without access to education.

Many also told the BBC there was only one hospital partially operational, opening a few days a week to perform critical amputations.

The local population was living under a "full blockade" by Russian forces, according to Ukraine's Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha.

Ukraine says it has attempted to deliver supplies to the area but has not had success in recent months.

The Kremlin in September acknowledged that Oleshky was facing "a critical situation" and "problems with supplies of food and medicine", but added that "Russia's military was working to resolve them" and blamed Kyiv.

Oleshky was home to 24,000 people before Russia's full-scale invasion. Now Ukraine estimates that some 6,000 people remain in the city and its surrounding areas, including 200 children.

It is also one of a number of settlements where thousands of people lost their homes to a massive flooding caused by the collapse of Nova Khakovka Dam in 2023. Ukraine and its allies accused Russia of blowing up the dam, while Russia blamed Ukraine.

While the US first lady is relatively lower profile than some of her predecessors - and only occasionally seen at White House events - she has become involved in addressing humanitarian issues stemming from the Russia-Ukraine war.

In August 2025, Melania Trump penned a letter to Putin, telling him it was "time to protect children and future generations worldwide".

Although she did not mention Ukraine by name, just days later at the White House Zelensky handed over a letter from his wife Olena, thanking her for her efforts on children.

In a rare public appearance in October the same year, the US first lady said that Putin had answered directly in writing and that her representatives were working with the Russian president's team to repatriate Ukrainian children from Russia and vice versa.

Some 34 children have reportedly been returned since 2025, including five this July.

According to US President Donald Trump, his wife has also privately expressed scepticism about Putin and his desire to achieve peace.

"I'd get home, I'd say, 'First lady, I had the most wonderful talk with Vladimir. I think we're finished'," Trump said in July last year.

"And then I'll turn on the television, or she'll say to me one time, 'Wow, that's strange because they just bombed a nursing home.'"

articles.title: Make universities limit ties to China — and fund US STEM students instead
articles.summary: The U.S. must attract the most talented foreign academics and researchers, but it cannot open its doors to students with direct links to the Chinese Communist Party.
articles.body:
The War Department announcement that thirty universities have “fully mitigated” their relationships with “foreign entities of concern” — most notably Chinese academic institutions — is a welcome development. These “entities” appear on the latest update to the list mandated by the 2019 National Defense Authorization Act to identify “foreign institutions engaging in problematic activities.”

The department’s latest update of the list identified 130 such institutions “located in China, Russia and Iran” whose activities enable “adversarial government interference.”

Not surprisingly, the department’s latest announcement has met some skepticism if not outright opposition from some of the thirty universities that have agreed to mitigation. Several have announced that they will not cut all ties with China; after all, “mitigated” is not the same as “terminated.”

The universities’ reaction should come as no surprise. For years, American institutions of higher learning and their supporters have argued that cooperation with their foreign counterparts is critical to advancing cutting-edge research. As a 2025 letter from the Asian American Scholar Forum to the chairmen and ranking members of the Armed Services Committees put it , “critical to our research enterprise is our ability to attract and retain the best global talents, foster international collaborations, and reduce the chilling effect on the Asian American and broader research community.”

This has been especially true with respect to the longstanding debate over restricting the number of Chinese students attending U.S. universities — an issue over which the American public is evenly divided . In fact, the number of Chinese students attending American universities declined during the past decade from a peak of 370,000 in 2018 to 266,000 in the 2024-2025 academic year. But that is still a significant number.

As Rep. John Moolenaar (R-Mich.), chairman of the House Select Committee on China, outlined in a recent letter to Secretary Pete Hegseth, many Chinese students receive their support—and can pay full tuition — from the China Scholarship Council, which targets “STEM disciplines aligned with China’s industrial policies and medium to long-term development plans [and is] a key channel for transferring human talent, intellectual capital, and technical expertise back to [China] in support of its national strategic objectives.”

Moreover, Moolenaar notes, the council requires sponsored students to submit regular reports to Chinese authorities “detailing their academic progress, laboratory work, research outputs and publications,” to return to China after competing their studies, and to serve in government afterward for at least two years.

For these reasons, Moolenaar demands that the War Department “prohibit any researcher, graduate student, postdoctoral researcher or other research personnel receiving funding or financial support from the China Scholarship Council from participating” in research funded by the department. This would no doubt result in a further decline in the number of Chinese students attending American institutions of higher learning.

Those who oppose such restrictions go so far as to claim that “banning Chinese students would cast the strategic competition with China as a racially motivated action … banning an entire group of citizens from Asia would not only light a match under our relations with China, it would also outrage several of our close allies around the region.”

But Moolenaar’s letter does not call for a ban on all Chinese students, nor is the argument for reducing their number racially motivated. On the contrary, there is much to be said for welcoming foreign researchers, whatever their race, to study in the U.S. and collaborate with, American university programs — especially those related to cutting-edge technologies. As a member of the Congressionally mandated National Security Commission on Emerging Biotechnology , I have met throughout the U.S. with leading researchers who have made breakthroughs on the most advanced biotechnology projects; many of them are non-white first-generation Americans.

The U.S. must continue to attract the most talented foreign academics and researchers if it is to remain the world’s leading source of technological innovation. But it cannot open its doors to students who have direct links to the Chinese government and the Chinese Communist Party. That would contribute to Beijing’s tireless effort to replace the U.S. as the world’s technological leader.

Instead, as I suggested five years ago , the Pentagon should set aside funds to expand its scholarship programs for students who until now could not attend the university programs of their choice because they could not afford to pay for them and were displaced by Chinese students who could.

In that way, not only would the War Department prevent Beijing’s exploitation of our intellectual resources, but by supporting an expanded pool of talented young Americans hoping to pursue careers in advanced technology, it also would further strengthen the nation’s intellectual and technological security.

Dov S. Zakheim is a senior adviser at the Center for Strategic and International Studies and vice chairman of the board for the Foreign Policy Research Institute. He was under secretary of Defense (comptroller) and chief financial officer for the Department of Defense from 2001 to 2004 and a deputy under secretary of Defense from 1985 to 1987.

articles.title: Kushner pushes back on report involving phone, spies, transfer
articles.summary: An excerpt from an upcoming book claims Kushner had access to alleged Middle Eastern "slush" funds when he served as a senior White House adviser during the...
articles.body:
Jared Kushner is pushing back on a report involving a hacked iPhone, international spies and billion-dollar transfers from foreign governments.

An upcoming book by journalist Matthew Cole claims Kushner, who is President Trump's son-in-law, had access to more than $2 billion in "slush money funds" from Middle Eastern leaders in an attempt to influence U.S. foreign policy.

An excerpt of the book released Thursday details allegations encompassing Kushner's time as a senior White House adviser during the first Trump administration, which included a lead role in U.S. policy in the Middle East. Kushner had a major hand in negotiating key foreign policy deals that involved Israel, the Gulf states, China and Russia during that period.

Kushner and his legal team released fiery statements Thursday night categorically denying all accusations against him. Kushner said , "The allegations made by this author are completely insane and never happened." His attorney called them "false and defamatory" and said they intend to pursue legal action against those responsible, but did not specify whom.

The new book, "Princes and Thieves: Jared Kushner and Mohamed bin Zayed's Secret Plot to Remake the Middle East," alleges Kushner had access to billions of dollars in undisclosed foreign bank accounts intended to pay for "influence within the U.S. government."

An excerpt from the book that was published in "Vanity Fair," but not independently verified by CBS News, says Dutch intelligence agents learned the Russians had hacked Kushner's iPhone in 2017 after flipping a Russian spy and subsequently gained access to Kushner's phone as well.

According to the report, "when Kushner used the phone, they could see his screen. Almost as soon as they got inside, the intelligence service began capturing every image of Kushner's screen as he used it."

At the time, Kushner served as a senior White House adviser to President Trump, including on Middle Eastern diplomacy.

The report alleges Dutch spies witnessed him log into a United Arab Emirates account that had allegedly received hundreds of millions of dollars from a bank in Azerbaijan, and claims the leaders of Saudi Arabia and the UAE put at least $2 billion into multiple bank accounts linked to Kushner, including an account with Israel's Central Bank.

According to the book excerpt, the owners and managers of the accounts were often disguised as official government entities or charities, but the funds were actually intended for "off-the-books diplomatic objectives" such as striking a deal to end the Israeli-Palesteinian conflict.

The report also claims Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman put roughly $1 billion into at least one account for Kushner, citing a "person with knowledge of the money" saying "its allocation was for Kushner's personal benefit."

Kushner forcefully denied the accusations leveled in the "Vanity Fair" excerpt, writing in part, "The allegations made by this author are completely insane and never happened."

"We denied every claim on the record, yet the author provided not a single shred of verifiable evidence to substantiate them," he said.

"No bank statements, wire transfer records, account numbers, transaction dates, or other verifiable details were provided to support these extraordinary accusations," he said.

CBS News reached out to the White House, which referred us to a statement from Steven Cheung, who is assistant to the president and White House director of communications.

Cheung said the "bull**** Vanity Fair article comes from a book that is complete fiction, and was fabricated from the warped mind of failed spy thriller writer."

"He presents no evidence or even a shred of documentation. Just mysterious words from unnamed sources," Cheung said on X.

articles.title: Trump election advisers donate Bosnia consulting fee to presidential library
articles.summary: President Trump’s political advisers James Blair and Chris LaCivita confirmed Friday they donated their full fee from their consulting work for a pro-Russian political party in Bosnia-Herzegovina to Trump’s presidential library. “Yes, it’s true we donated our full fee. I love the President and am eternally grateful for the opportunities he has provided me,” Blair said…
articles.body:
President Trump’s political advisers James Blair and Chris LaCivita confirmed Friday they donated their full fee from their consulting work for a pro-Russian political party in Bosnia-Herzegovina to Trump’s presidential library.

“Yes, it’s true we donated our full fee. I love the President and am eternally grateful for the opportunities he has provided me,” Blair said in a post on the social platform X, referring to the New York Post story that was first to report on the donation.

“Contributing to the preservation of his legacy of greatness is my honor!” Blair said.

LaCivita reposted Blair, writing “preserving the legacy and story of @realDonaldTrump is an honor and a no brainer!”

The Trump Presidential Library and Museum is expected to be housed in Miami, Fla.

The donations come after Trump warned earlier this month he would terminate Blair and LaCivita if their work in the Balkans conflicted with the White House.

“Chris LaCivita and James Blair are outside consultants. They do not work for me, other than as outside consultants,” Trump wrote in a post on Truth Social. “They most likely have numerous clients, but for that, you would have to ask them.”

“They are allowed to do work for others, just like all consultants in Washington, D.C.,” he continued. “I do not have any idea who else they work for but will, on reflection, ask them and, if there’s a conflict, I will terminate them, immediately!”

articles.title: Trump says he ordered the Justice Department's lawsuit over Alaska's US Senate race
articles.summary: President Donald Trump on Friday said he told his administration to file its lawsuit to block certification of the U. Senate race in Alaska if Republican Sen...
articles.body:
President Donald Trump on Friday said he told his administration to file its lawsuit to block certification of the U.S. Senate race in Alaska if Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan loses, kicking off what many fear could become a lengthy battle between the government and states over certifying an election where the president's party is struggling.

"I'm the one that said do it," Trump told reporters as he landed for a campaign rally in Florida.

The lawsuit, filed late Thursday, centers on one of the president's longstanding complaints in the Senate race — the presence of a second candidate named Dan Sullivan who Republican fear could siphon away votes from the incumbent in what's likely to be a photo-finish contest with Democrat Mary Peltola, the state's former congresswoman.

The second Dan Sullivan, who is Daniel J. Sullivan from the tiny fishing community of Petersburg , has said he decided to run on his own, but Republicans have contended he is a Democratic plant to siphon votes away from their candidate.

The lawsuit by the Republican president's Department of Justice in federal court in Alaska demands that the state be blocked from certifying a Peltola win if Daniel J. Sullivan remains on the ballot. "The United States accordingly brings this lawsuit to protect the integrity of the 2026 Senate election in Alaska," the lawsuit says, contending that federal law requires states to protect the integrity of federal elections.

The legal challenge came 11 days before the Nov. 3 election and months after the final ballot was set.

The Alaska Supreme Court rejected a previous Republican effort to remove Daniel J. Sullivan from the ballot, and the state's Republican officials made the decisions about how to list him on the ballot. He will appear without a party designation next to his name, while the senator will be listed as the Republican incumbent. Alaska's ranked choice voting system also will allow voters to select both of the men if confused.

Peltola and Sen. Sullivan were top vote-getters in nonpartisan primary

The senator received more than 68,000 votes in the August primary, while the challenging Sullivan got 4,107, about 2% of the total vote. Peltola, who had previously served one term in the House, was the top vote-getter in the nonpartisan primary. Both parties expect that whoever wins in November will do so by a tight margin in a state of 738,000 people.

The campaign for Sen. Dan Sullivan did not address whether the senator supports the Department of Justice's intervention. "We'll let the DOJ complaint run its course," campaign spokesman Nate Adams said in a text message. "Alaskans can tell the difference between a Democrat sideshow and Senator Sullivan's strong record of delivering for Alaska."

Daniel J. Sullivan, whose presence on the ballot is at issue in the lawsuit, did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

"Donald Trump knows that Dan Sullivan is going to lose the election, so now his Department of Justice is filing a sham lawsuit to overturn the will of Alaska voters and steal an election when he loses," said Devan Barber, executive director of the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee.

In a statement on Friday, the Department of Justice noted that Alaska's election officials, who are Republicans, determined the other Sullivan's campaign was an attempt to "mislead:" voters and wanted him removed from the ballot. Both a state court and Alaska's Supreme Court disagreed and kept the second Sullivan on the ballot.

"The Justice Department, consistent with the National Voter Registration Act enacted by Congress, is taking the necessary steps to ensure that this frivolous candidacy does not undermine the integrity of Alaska's election or the will of its voters," the DoJ statement said.

The Department of Justice has increasingly been used to bolster the president's political operation, targeting his enemies and suing Democratic-controlled states before the election. Democrats and many voting rights advocates have long feared that the administration will try to block certification of elections that Trump's party loses, much as he unsuccessfully tried to do when he lost the White House race to Democrat Joe Biden.

U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche said that was unlikely outside of extreme circumstances. "It is not DOJ's intention to, and it's never our intention to, improperly interfere with elections or the state certification process," he told reporters Thursday in Virginia before the lawsuit was filed.

The lawsuit was signed by Associate U.S. Attorney General Stanley Woodward, who represented Trump allies and Jan. 6 defendants before becoming one of the top appointees at the department.

Constitution gives states the power to run elections

Derek Muller, a law professor at the University of Notre Dame, said the lawsuit would likely only kick in if Republicans narrowly lost the Alaska Senate race and that it probably would not survive long. "The statute simply doesn't let the Department of Justice enjoin certification," Muller said. "The lawsuit could well be mooted by a wide Democratic victory or a narrow Republican one, and if not, the court will likely dismiss it next month."

The U.S. Constitution grants states the power to run their own elections. Elections for federal office like the Senate must comply with standards set by Congress. That division of power has frustrated Trump, who repeatedly has tried to seize control of election procedures through executive orders that courts have blocked .

The final step for a state election is formally certifying the winner, the act that the administration's lawsuit seeks to prevent, it requests, "pending an investigation to determine whether votes cast for. Daniel J. Sullivan were meant to be cast for Senator Sullivan."

The process in Alaska is complicated by the state's ranked choice voting system, which Trump opposes, and many expect it to take weeks before a winner is known. Also on the state's ballot is an initiative to repeal that system.

Trump has stepped up complaints about a ballot with dueling Sullivans

Trump has complained about Daniel J. Sullivan's presence on the ballot, making reference to it during a rally in Alaska this month and in repeated social media posts, including one this week where he called it "CHEATING."

"We are looking at powerful legal options to remove the fraudulent Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. from the Ballot, and holding the Democrats accountable for their Election Interference, in the pursuit of Justice and Fairness," the president wrote on Wednesday.

Clogging a ballot with third party candidates to siphon off votes from the other major party is a long-standing tactic in the country's two-party system. Republicans have been linked to an effort to persuade Ohio voters to support a socialist in that state's Senate race, which could help Republican Sen. Jon Husted fend off a challenge from former Democratic Sen. Sherrod Brown.

Associated Press writer Ali Swenson in New York and Alanna Durkin Richer in Washington, DC contributed to this report.

articles.title: America’s health insurance model crumbles under the success of modern medicine
articles.summary: We are trying to pay for 21st-century medical miracles with a mid-20th-century financing model. It’s time for a change.
articles.body:
Every fall, millions of Americans sit down for the same grim ritual: open enrollment. The insurance logos are familiar, and the email from HR still insists the company is “committed to offering competitive benefits.” Then the sticker shock sets in.

Heading into 2027, employer plan costs are projected to jump 9.5 percent , pushing the average past $19,000 per worker. On the Affordable Care Act marketplaces, insurers have proposed a median premium hike of 15 percent . And for millions buying their own coverage, the math has stopped working altogether. Over the last year, individual market enrollment plunged by more than 4.5 million people — dropping 18 percent from 25.2 million in 2025 to 20.5 million in mid-2026. Driven by the expiration of COVID-era enhanced tax credits and recent federal policy shifts, it is the steepest drop in a decade.

When premiums spike and millions lose coverage, it is easy to blame insurers, hospital monopolies or drugmakers. They bear plenty of responsibility. But the deeper failure is structural: Our health insurance model is an artifact of an era when medicine didn’t actually work very well.

Tying health insurance to employment and paying for it with pre-tax dollars is an accidental byproduct of World War II wage controls. Back then, medical care was rudimentary. Outside of setting a bone or delivering a baby, you mostly went to the hospital to die. Because effective interventions were rare, pooling risk through the workplace to cover the occasional hospital stay made sense.

Eighty years later, medicine works remarkably well. We have targeted biologics, gene therapies, and revolutionary drugs like GLP-1s that fundamentally alter the trajectory of chronic disease. Millions of people can, and should, take these therapies for a lifetime to stay healthy.

The catch is you cannot finance a lifetime of expensive maintenance therapies for half the population through an insurance mechanism built for rare, unpredictable accidents. Insurance works when a large group pays a little each month to protect against a catastrophe that hits an unlucky few. When almost everyone needs ongoing care to stay healthy, the traditional risk pool breaks.

As the system buckles under the weight of new treatments and provider consolidation, employers and insurers fall back on their only playbook: shifting costs onto workers. Deductibles climb so high that millions of Americans are insured on paper, yet avoid the doctor because they cannot afford the bill.

Fixing this demands structural reform. We must retire our obsolete employer-sponsored model and rebuild healthcare financing around two distinct pillars.

First, we implement universal catastrophic protection. Insurance should go back to being actual insurance. Every American should have baseline catastrophic coverage — detached from employment — that protects families from the financial ruin of a cancer diagnosis, a major surgery, an intensive care unit stay, or a million-dollar gene therapy.

Second, we need a transparent cash market for routine and preventive care. For everyday medicine — primary care, diagnostics and routine maintenance medications — we should remove the insurance middleman. Routing predictable care through third-party payers adds massive administrative bloat while hiding real prices behind opaque insurer-provider negotiations.

When providers and drugmakers have to compete directly for consumer dollars, prices fall fast. Look at what has happened with GLP-1s. While insurers scrambled to restrict coverage and employers balked at the cost, a direct-to-consumer cash market emerged. Over the last two years, fierce competition for cash-paying patients has driven the price of GLP-1 treatments down from more than $1,500 a month to starting prices around $150 a month .

That is what happens when incentives align. Transparent competition replaces bureaucratic rationing, and care actually becomes affordable.

To accelerate this transition, policymakers should stop funneling hundreds of billions of dollars in pre-tax subsidies exclusively into bloated, employer-chosen plans. Instead, tax advantages should go directly to individuals to pair portable catastrophic coverage with flexible accounts they can spend on routine, preventive cash-pay care. In the near term, lawmakers should also mandate that whenever a patient pays cash for a service at or below their insurer’s negotiated rate, that spending must count toward their annual deductible.

We are trying to pay for 21st-century medical miracles with a mid-20th-century financing model. As 4.5 million Americans fall off the individual marketplaces and employer costs surge past $19,000 per worker, the cracks in the foundation are impossible to ignore. It is time to build universal protection for the medical catastrophes that could bankrupt us, and unleash transparent cash markets for the everyday care that keeps us healthy.

Michael Botta is a healthcare economist and co-founder of Sesame.

articles.summary: Two former FBI officials who have come under withering criticism from allies of President Donald Trump over their intelligence work during the 2020 presidential election have been charged with allegedly lying to Congress.
articles.body: WASHINGTON — Two former FBI officials who have come under withering criticism from allies of President Donald Trump have been charged with allegedly lying to Congress over the investigation into former President Joe Biden’s son Hunter Biden. A court docket shows that Nikki Floris, the former deputy assistant director of the FBI’s Counterintelligence Division, and Bradley Benavides, another FBI official, were facing one count of the rarely-charged criminal offense which can be difficult to prosecute. The case was brought through a criminal complaint. They have not yet been indicted by a federal grand jury in D.C., where grand jurors have been skeptical of cases brought during Trump’s second term. She joined the FBI as an intelligence analyst in 2005, working on the director’s daily briefing staff and helped produce intelligence documents. Floris has also been under criticism from Republicans over emails in which she discussed intelligence work that were obtained by Congress and declassified in July by Trump. Republicans have alleged that FBI officials buried what they describe as a credible report on China’s efforts to influence the election in an effort to protect then-FBI Director Christopher Wray. Intelligence officials and her legal team have said the pullback was a standard administrative move for a report that may have been unverified or had flawed intelligence.

articles.title: Chicago's 12-language ballots make elections 'harder to monitor,' Illinois GOP chair warns
articles.summary: Illinois Republican Party chairman warns Chicago's 12-language ballot system is "big city virtue signaling" that creates oversight gaps for election judges.
articles.body: Chicago voters can cast ballots in 12 different languages this election, an expansion that Illinois Republican Party Chairman Bob Grogan warns is making an already complicated election system harder to independently monitor. Grogan told Fox News Digital the proliferation of versions in languages such as Tagalog, Gujarati and Urdu creates additional challenges for election judges and party observers tasked with ensuring voters receive accurate ballots. He also questioned how many voters need some of the translations, arguing that many immigrants who speak those languages also speak English. "It's a solution in search of a problem," Grogan told Fox News Digital. "It's big city virtue signaling." TRUMP ADMIN SUED OVER ALLEGED ILLEGAL COLLECTION OF SENSITIVE VOTER DATA FROM 47 STATES Chicago voters can cast ballots in 12 different languages: English, Spanish, Chinese, Hindi, Korean, Tagalog, Polish, Gujarati, Urdu, Ukrainian, Arabic and Russian. Section 203 of the U.S. Voting Rights Act requires the Chicago Board of Elections to make materials and ballots available in certain precincts for Spanish, Chinese and Hindi speakers, a spokesperson for the elections agency told Fox News Digital. The Board includes the other non-English languages to "maintain uniformity with the languages used by the Cook County Clerk's office under a county ordinance, so that all voters throughout Cook County are afforded equal voting opportunities," the spokesperson added. But Grogan, a former DuPage County auditor for 12 years, said he has "a fair number of Gujarati friends ... and everyone in their family speaks English." "Gujarati — it's from India, and English is an official language in India," Grogan added. TRUMP ADMIN'S PROPOSED 'ENGLISH-ONLY' HEAD START RULE DRAWS FIRE FROM LOS ANGELES MAYORAL CANDIDATE Data provided to Fox News Digital by the Chicago Board of Elections shows that some of the less commonly used language options accounted for only a handful of ballots cast during the March primary. Just nine ballots were cast using the English-Gujarati option, while 15 used English-Urdu, 10 used English-Arabic and 25 each used English-Russian and English-Ukrainian, according to the Board's figures. Other translations were used more frequently, including 4,474 English-Polish ballots, 2,183 English-Chinese ballots, 664 English-Hindi ballots, 352 English-Korean ballots and 100 English-Tagalog ballots. Grogan also questioned why language requirements can change substantially across county lines, noting that Chicago offers touchscreen ballots in 12 languages while nearby DuPage County offers fewer language options. "You can have a Gujarati population in Peoria," Grogan said. "You would think that there would be some more uniformity to all of that as well." SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER Beyond questioning the need for some of the translations, Grogan raised a broader concern about oversight, arguing that election judges and party observers cannot independently scrutinize ballots written in languages they do not understand. However, the Chicago Board of Elections pushed back, telling Fox News Digital that it has in-house staff who help translate ballots and signs and assist multilingual media ahead of elections. It also said voters are allowed to bring "interpreter[s] to assist them in understanding and casting their ballot" under certain conditions. When asked about multilingual judges, the Board noted that of the 7,218 election judges assigned for November's general election as of Thursday, 810 are multilingual candidates. Those multilingual judges include speakers of Spanish, Chinese, Hindi, Urdu, Gujarati, Polish, Korean and Tagalog, according to the Board. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Pressed on whether he believes the additional languages create an election security vulnerability, Grogan said the risk depends in part on how widely the translated ballots are used. Overall, the Board's figures show 7,857 multilingual ballots were cast during the March primary, representing about 1.85% of the 424,564 ballots cast citywide. "I think it certainly makes it harder to monitor," Grogan said. "If there is one ballot cast in that language, that's a very small vulnerability you have. If all of a sudden we have 10,000 in some very small, poorly understood language, then that increases the risk." Fox News Digital asked the Chicago Board of Elections how many languages are available for mail-in ballots but did not receive a response in time for publication.

articles.body:
The son of GOP Rep. Ralph Norman (S.C.), Warren Norman, said Friday he is “leaning” toward supporting the Democratic candidate in South Carolina’s Senate race, pediatrician Annie Andrews.

Ralph Norman, who was defeated by Sen. Darline Graham (R-S.C.) in the GOP primary, said in a radio interview this week he would back the Republican nominee in the November election but indicated that his family would not vote for her.

The Republican’s son made it official in an op-ed published in South Carolina outlet FITSNews, titled “Why This Lifelong Conservative Won’t Vote for Darline Graham.”

Warren Norman noted in his piece that the decision was not “personal,” extending his sympathy to Graham following the loss of her brother, the late Sen. Lindsey Graham (R-S.C.).

However, he claimed that there was “no true conservative to vote for in this election.”

“If Senator Graham wins, the establishment that backed her will protect her in every primary to come,” Norman wrote. “This seat could be hers for 24 years or more.

“If Annie Andrews wins and doesn’t stand up to her party the way she has promised, South Carolina voters can hold her accountable and replace her with a strong conservative in six,” he continued. “Six years we can hold accountable, or 24 years we can’t. To me, that isn’t a hard call.”

The Republican lawmaker’s son indicated that he was considering a vote for the Democratic nominee in the race instead. Despite disagreeing with Andrews “a lot,” the real estate partner said they agree “on some important things,” like opposing corruption and insurance reform.

“She struck me as genuine, and she has said publicly that she’ll stand up to her own party,” Norman wrote. “That is the standard I’m asking of every candidate, and I intend to hold her to it.

“As of today, I’m leaning her way,” he continued. “It will be the first time in my life I’ve voted for a Democrat in a partisan election.”

Andrews responded to Norman’s op-ed in a statement to The Hill on Friday.

“South Carolinians deserve a senator who earns their vote, not someone handpicked by the same Washington insiders driving up our costs,” the Democratic candidate said. “Whether you voted for Donald Trump, Lindsey Graham, or anyone else, if you care more about lowering your bills than the political games in Washington, this campaign is for you.”

The Hill has reached out to Graham’s campaign for comment.

articles.title: Home distillers rejoice as US Supreme Court considers whether moonshine
articles.summary: The Supreme Court will consider in the new year whether the 1868 legislation forbidding home distilling should be overturned.
articles.body:
Wyoming mechanic and amateur moonshiner Geno Stecks proudly details the modifications he's made at his two-bedroom residence to facilitate his hobby of distilling liquor in his own home.

"I turned my dining room into my shining room," boasted the bearded 66-year-old, who uses a power drill fixed to a bowl to mix some of his recipe.

Two years ago, he began tinkering with recipes for home-producing spirits. The pastime has taught him new skills and given him a signature product to share with friends and neighbors - "coffee-flavoured shine". It also happens to be illegal under US law.

"You know, keep quiet - don't make commercials or nothing," Stecks said.

But some home distillers hope they won't have to keep their hobby a secret for longer. The Supreme Court announced this week that it would reconsider the 1868 legislation forbidding the practice, and hobby distillers hope that their spirits will soon be treated like beer and wine, which are both legal to brew at home across the country.

Plaintiffs who brought the cases say Congress overstepped its powers in restricting distilling for tax purposes during the Reconstruction era. They want the highest judges in the country to agree.

But lawyers for the government argue that Congress's measure was lawful, and necessary to stop producers from avoiding taxes.

One lower court found the almost 160-year-old ban unconstitutional, but in a separate and similar case, another lower court came to the opposite conclusion. The Supreme Court will hear the case early next year and could make a ruling in the summer of 2027.

Currently, distilling alcohol in a private home carries a penalty of up to five years in prison, a $10,000 (£7,460) fine or both.

"The particular law in question here is both absurd and unconstitutional," said lawyer Robert Alt, representing the plaintiffs. "It's interesting to note that this is a hobby which is as American as apple pie - and certainly a lot older."

Alt, Stecks and many proponents of the change point out that George Washington himself distilled spirits at home. Historian Daniel Pierce told the BBC that home distilling was first criminalised for revenue purposes, requiring anyone making spirits to pay a tax.

When federal agents began enforcing the law, small farmers who were distilling on the side as a way to make some extra money or to barter were left with few options.

"If you're a large distiller or something, you could afford to [pay the tax], but for most people, it was out of the question," Pierce said.

When the US implemented Prohibition - the nationwide ban on the production and sale of alcohol between 1930 and 1933 - it created a whole new market for illegal distillers, particularly moonshiners, Pierce said.

NASCAR, the racing sport, was born out of the high-speed, modified cars that bootleggers once used to transport illicit liquor and outrun the law.

Many continued their illegal distilling after Prohibition's end, often passing on family recipes in secret (or, at least, in tightly-knit circles) for generations.

Then moonshine and home distilling enjoyed a new renaissance in the early 2000s, he said, thanks to reality TV shows like Moonshiners, the internet and popular culture.

"You start to get this pretty dramatic revival…. in terms of home distilling," Pierce said.

Rick Morris, the founder and president of the Hobby Distillers Association, was one of the challengers who sued in Texas to change the law. He first entered the drinks industry working with soda machines and bottled water, then became a hobbyist home brewer of beer and wine with his wife.

They made a frustrating discovery when they tried to take the "next step" into distilling.

"It didn't make sense," he said. "I could make beer, I could make wine, both perfectly legally … and it was frustrating that I couldn't take what I had already legally made and do one more step to it, to start to try to make a bourbon or a brandy."

The allure for Morris and many other hobbyists, they say, is the mechanics and innovation behind the process.

"There is a lot of science and details to get straightened out, but there is still a big vein of creativity in the art that goes into it - blending flavours and aromas and all that," said Ohio challenger John Bream, an aerospace engineer by trade.

He first took up the hobby when his wife gave him a home-brewing kit around 17 years ago. He set up his operations in their kitchen but "made too many messes and got kicked out into the garage".

"Through homebrewing, I became aware that going to the next level of distilling was illegal … so I stayed away from it," he said.

But he realised he could be "part of the force for good" by joining legal challenges to the archaic law.

Not everyone is on board with the move, Courtney Armour, chief legal officer at The Distilled Spirits Council of the US, told the BBC. She worries about the challenges and dangers that come with home producing.

"The distillation process can be quite dangerous, including risk of explosion, burns, fires, and more," Armour said. "The spirits industry has a clear focus on safety and process management to mitigate these risks, but even in that careful environment there are still accidents, injuries and even fatalities."

And then there are health concerns that can arise when alcohol has not been produced properly.

"In a home-distilling setting, these dangers would not just be limited to the individuals engaging in the production but also their neighbors in the surrounding area," Armour said.

While home distilling remains federally banned, states like Missouri and New Hampshire have passed legislation allowing the production of certain amounts at home for personal consumption.

Attorney Alt pointed out that "alcohol, traditionally, has been an area of state regulation … so this question of state versus federal authority is really at the very heart of this case".

Alt also said the legal challenge addresses what oversight federal authorities have on home activities.

"This circuit court said, look, if the federal government is right on this, there's almost no limits to what they could ban at home in the name of taxation," he said.

Distillery owner and former Missouri state representative Don Gosen said he helped shape the state's 1995 law allowing residents to distill 100 gallons of spirits at home per year per person - or 200 gallons per household.

"I've never seen the federal government come and fine anybody for doing it, because it's kind of small potatoes … and so a lot of people, I believe, still do it, kind of behind the scenes like in the old days," Gosen said.

Many people have come to him for advice over the years, not knowing about the federal law. Some bring him their homemade bottles and ask his opinion, he said.

"I'll taste it, and it'll be terrible," Gosen laughed. "And I'll throw on a happy face and say, 'Oh, it's wonderful' - because they made it. They love it."

Gosen, Morris and others within the industry believe legally allowing home distilling will only help it grow.

"Home interest generally turns into a better consumer, a more educated consumer, a more sophisticated consumer, just a consumer that spends more," Gosen said. "You're going to have people like myself that are going to start opening our doors to home distillers and have classes for them and help them out."

Back in Wyoming, moonshiner mechanic Stecks agrees that more people will start home distilling if they don't risk penalties and prison - and sees only growth and good things coming from legalisation.

articles.title: Buttigieg endorses independent in Montana Senate race with a Democrat still on the ballot
articles.summary: Former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg endorsed independent Seth Bodnar on Friday over the Democratic nominee in Montana’s Senate race. Buttigieg’s endorsement of Bodnar, first reported by ABC News, is the latest in a string of Democratic efforts to swing the race toward the independent candidate, who some believe has a better chance to beat Republican…
articles.body:
Former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg endorsed independent Seth Bodnar on Friday over the Democratic nominee in Montana’s Senate race.

Buttigieg’s endorsement of Bodnar, first reported by ABC News , is the latest in a string of Democratic efforts to swing the race toward the independent candidate, who some believe has a better chance to beat Republican Kurt Alme. Democrat Alani Bankhead has received numerous calls to drop out of the race in order to clear the field for Bodnar but has refused .

“The best leaders I’ve served with, in uniform and in government, care more about getting the job done than about who gets the credit, and Seth is one of them,” Buttigieg said in a statement.

The potential 2028 presidential candidate acknowledged that he and Bodnar do not agree on everything but said the independent has spent his life serving the country, which Buttigieg said Bodnar would continue to do in the Senate.

Although it is notable for a national Democrat to endorse against the party’s nominee, Bodnar has received a swath of Democratic support, including from former Sen. Jon Tester (D-Mont.). Shannon O’Brien, chair of the Montana Democratic Party, resigned from her position earlier this month and endorsed Bodnar.

“Montana deserves a senator who will fight corruption in Washington, defend reproductive freedom, and work across the aisle to lower costs and actually get things done. Seth Bodnar will be that Senator,” Buttigieg wrote.

Bankhead has said she will not drop out of the race, and even if she did, Montana law would require the party to put forth a new nominee. Democrats deciding to back independent candidates has become a trend in this year’s midterm races, with many Democrats in Nebraska, South Dakota and Idaho supporting a candidate outside the two-party system.

Bodnar told ABC News that he was honored to have Buttigieg’s endorsement and proud that people “across the political spectrum” were joining his campaign.

Montana’s Senate race is deemed “likely Republican” by election handicapper Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ). DDHQ’s polling average shows Alme ahead with 41.9 percent support, Bodnar with 29.4 percent and Bankhead with 17.1 percent as of Friday morning.

articles.title: Justice Department sues to block Alaska results if Sullivan loses
articles.summary: The Trump administration has filed a lawsuit that aims to block certification of the Senate election in Alaska if incumbent Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan loses his reelection bid. The lawsuit, filed Thursday in the U.S. District Court for the district of Alaska, argues that a win for Democrat Mary Peltola could be blocked by the…
articles.body:
The Trump administration has filed a lawsuit that aims to block certification of the Senate election in Alaska if incumbent Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan loses his reelection bid.

The lawsuit, filed Thursday in the U.S. District Court for the district of Alaska, argues that a win for Democrat Mary Peltola could be blocked by the controversial appearance on the ballot of a candidate with the same name as the incumbent.

The filing alleges that Daniel J. Sullivan, who goes by Dan Sullivan, entered the race as a Republican “with the intention of misleading” the incumbent’s supporters, and that his inclusion on the ballot would cause voter confusion.

“Should Alaska certify any electoral results tainted by the inclusion on the ballot of Daniel J. Sullivan … the State and its officers will fail in its obligation to protect the integrity of its election,” the filing reads.

The fight for control of the Senate could come down to Alaska this fall. The Last Frontier is considered a solidly red state that President Trump won by double digits in the last presidential race, but Peltola narrowly leads in recent polls of Senate fight.

Decision Desk HQ’s polling averages put Peltola up by roughly 2 percentage points over Sullivan, with a “lean Democratic” forecast. Cook Political Report still considers the race a “toss up,” with early voting underway.

Alaska Division of Elections Director Carol Beecher launched an investigation earlier this year into Daniel J. Sullivan’s run, citing “credible allegations” that he was running as a spoiler and concluded that he couldn’t appear on the ballot.

She noted the political newcomer’s recent switch to the Republican Party and his ties to a political consultant for Peltola, though Peltola’s camp has said it has no involvement with either Sullivan campaign.

Daniel J. Sullivan appealed to the Superior Court, arguing that Alaskan law does not regulate the “private motivations that draw individuals to declare or campaign for office.”

In a statement at the time, he contended that the attempts to remove him from the ballot “create the impression that the state government is being used to protect an incumbent senator from facing competition at the ballot box.”

A Superior Court judge eventually ruled that the challenger could remain on the ballot for the state’s Aug. 18 primary, from which both Sullivans advanced. But the Justice Department had reportedly launched an investigation into the Dan J. Sullivan campaign.

The ballots for next month’s general election list both “Dan S. Sullivan,” with a note highlighting his party and incumbent status, and “Daniel J. Sullivan Jr,” who is listed without a party affiliation.

Alaska uses ranked-choice voting for the general election.

“We’ll let the DOJ complaint run its course,” the senator Sullivan’s campaign spokesperson Nate Adams told The Hill in a statement. “Alaskans can tell the difference between a Democrat sideshow and Senator Sullivan’s strong record of delivering for Alaska, a record he’ll keep building on for the next six years.”

The Hill has also reached out to Dan J. Sullivan’s campaign.
