articles.body:
The United States Secret Service and D.C. police investigated reports of a “suspicious package” near the Ukrainian Embassy on Friday morning, according to a Secret Service statement provided to NewsNation.

Out of an “abundance of caution,” the 3300 block of M Street in Northwest D.C. and the Francis Scott Key Bridge were closed, according to the statement.

The Metropolitan Police Department (MPD), in a statement to NewsNation, said officers responded to assist the Secret Service in that area at 8:42 a.m. Friday after receiving reports of a “suspicious package.”

“MPD’s Explosive Ordnance Disposal Unit is responding to assist. The investigation is ongoing,” the statement said.

As of 11:20 a.m., MPD said the agency is clearing the location “with no hazardous materials found.”

The Ukrainian Embassy told NewsNation that the embassy was evacuated to “ensure the safety of embassy staff and visitors.”

The embassy said it has reopened, and consular services will resume shortly, as the item was deemed not harmful.

articles.title: ‘Foreign policy is the economy’: How Iran war is shaping US midterm vote
articles.summary: Democrats are framing the conflict as an affordability issue to criticise Republican candidates backed by Trump.
articles.body:
Detroit, Michigan – The first question in the United States Senate debate in Michigan between Democratic candidate Abdul El-Sayed and his Republican rival Mike Rogers was about the issue that appears to matter most to voters – the economy.

El-Sayed quickly drew a contrast between himself and Rogers, who is backed by US President Donald Trump. It was not about interest rates, taxes, or trade policy. It was about the US-Israel war on Iran .

“Right now, the cost of gas, the cost of groceries, it all really goes back to this war in Iran,” the progressive Democrat said on Wednesday.

“We need a War Powers Resolution rather than a senator who wants to stand hip-to-hip with Donald Trump on this war that made no sense when it started and certainly makes no sense now.”

El-Sayed was referring to legislative efforts to curb Trump’s ability to continue the eight-month conflict .

Across Michigan, Democrats are emphasising their opposition to the war to woo voters stung by rising gas and grocery prices.

“The war in Iran is a kitchen table issue,” said Jonathan Guyer, programme director at the Institute for Global Affairs (IGA).

“Voters don’t often rank foreign policy as their top issue, but I think it’s so interwoven with the economy right now that essentially foreign policy is the economy.”

IGA released a survey last month suggesting that 60 percent of potential voters disapprove of Trump’s handling of the war. More alarmingly for Republicans, an overwhelming majority of respondents – 81 percent – agreed that the conflict has raised the cost of living.

Almost immediately after Israel and the US started attacking Iran on February 28, Tehran began disrupting the flow of energy products through the Strait of Hormuz – sending oil and gas prices skyrocketing.

In the US, the price of diesel – which is used to power heavy machinery, including heavy trucks that ship consumer goods across the country – has reached record highs over the past weeks.

Likewise, petrol or gasoline has become less affordable. Average Americans feel that uptick firsthand almost daily at the gas pump.

The average price of one gallon (3.8 litres) of petrol has gone from less than $3 before the war to more than $4.27 as of Thursday, according to the American Automobile Association (AAA).

The increased cost of energy and transportation has trickled down to the entire economy, fuelling inflation at a time when affordability had become one of the key issues in US electoral politics.

Trump and his allies have argued that the war was necessary to prevent Iran from acquiring a nuclear weapon.

But before the war, Trump himself had said repeatedly that Iran’s nuclear programme had been “obliterated” by the June 2025 US strikes against the country’s uranium enrichment facilities.

And US intelligence officials have testified to Congress that they have no evidence that Iran is building a nuclear bomb.

Rogers, the Michigan Senate candidate, pushed to defend the war during the debate on Wednesday.

“You want to pay $8 [for] a gallon of gas, let Iran get a nuclear weapon. You lose control of that whole region,” he said.

At the same time, Rogers has also called for an end to the conflict.

In a recent campaign commercial filmed in a grocery store , the Republican candidate said, “The war with Iran needs to end, and end quickly.”

The position is echoed by other Republicans in tough House and Senate races.

In neighbouring Ohio, Senator Jon Husted has called for a “quick” end to the war as well. In Iowa, Congresswoman Ashley Hinson, who is running for the Senate, said she told Trump that the conflict should come to an “immediate and successful end”. In Maine, Senator Susan Collins has highlighted her vote in favour of several War Powers Resolutions.

Still, Trump, who is the leader of the Republican Party, has suggested that he may renew all-out fighting with Iran after the midterm vote next month, and he has promoted the war as a historic success.

“I think it’s one of the greatest things we’ve done. We’ve stopped Iran from having a nuclear weapon,” Trump told reporters on Wednesday.

“It’s one of the best things that we’ve done, and it took a lot of courage to do it because no other president was willing to do it.”

Despite the overall unpopularity of the war, most Republicans continue to support it.

A Pew Research Center poll released earlier this month showed that 63 percent of Republican respondents said they approve of Trump’s handling of the conflict.

The IGA survey, taken in August, put the number at 74 percent. But only 24 percent of Republican respondents said they “strongly approve” of Trump’s handling of the war – down from 40 percent in April.

Guyer suggested that the lack of enthusiastic support for the war in the Republican base may hurt the party in the upcoming elections.

“It means that Republicans aren’t necessarily walking away from the president, but their support for him has a lot less conviction,” he told Al Jazeera.

“That could have implications if they actually show up to vote [and] if they are going to be involved in campaigning.”

With the elections less than two weeks away, it’s apparent that the Democrats see the war as an Achilles heel for Republicans, and they are invoking the conflict incessantly to undermine Trump-backed candidates all over the country.

At a Senate debate watch party attended by dozens of El-Sayed’s supporters in Detroit on Wednesday, Al Jazeera asked Democratic Senator Chris Murphy – who recently returned from a visit to the Middle East – about the war. His answer was all about the US economy, not the geopolitics of the region.

“Well, diesel prices here in Detroit are already above $6 a gallon, and they’re going to go higher if this war restarts. Mike Rogers just said in the debate that he’s going to support the war, which is basically a death sentence for the American economy,” Murphy told Al Jazeera.

“There’s a big choice for Michigan voters to make here. If you want this war to continue for another year, if you want gas prices to climb to $8 a gallon, vote for Mike Rogers. If you want the war to end, if you want prices to come down, then vote for Abdul El-Sayed .”

Democratic Senator Chris Murphy addresses Abdul El-Sayed supporters at a debate watch party in Dearborn, Michigan, the US, October 21 [Ali Harb/Al Jazeera]

articles.title: Cognitive surrender: Artificial intelligence’s threat to democracy
articles.summary: Wesleyan University computer science professor Sebastian Zimmeck argues that artificial intelligence poses a threat to democratic citizenship by encouraging cognitive surrender and requiring both individual critical thinking and robust regulatory oversight to protect personal agency.
articles.body:
As a computer science faculty member at Wesleyan University, I am grappling alongside my colleagues with the impact of AI on student learning. In my department, we are currently restructuring the computer science major and drafting guidelines for AI in our curriculum.

A recent report from MIT noted that while AI chatbots can easily produce answers, they often trigger “cognitive surrender.” Indeed, in my own interactions with students, I realize that the issue is no longer just offloading homework; it is offloading thinking.

This development is concerning. Deliberate decision-making and personal autonomy are at the very foundations of democratic citizenship. Our democracy depends on citizens who can evaluate arguments, reason independently, and hold those in power accountable. When we let AI do this work for us, we risk our self-governance.

Current AI models are engineered for sycophancy. They confirm our biases while quietly steering our perspectives. They highlight select facts and suppress others, creating a dangerous opening for state control. At this year’s Privacy Enhancing Technologies Symposium, security expert John Scott-Railton described how autocratic governments are increasingly coercing tech companies into adopting “safety” frameworks that invisibly steer model responses.

Such manipulation is a potent tool to undermine civic engagement. Unlike traditional censorship, which flatly prohibits speech and overtly blocks content, algorithmic steering quietly neutralizes dissent and pacifies civic debate before it even has a chance to manifest. This new form of censorship does not forbid us to speak; it prevents us from thinking.

To be sure, advertisers and politicians have manipulated human desires for ages. However, generative AI poses a new threat to democratic deliberation. Because we interact with these models as if they were empathetic and all-knowing confidants, their persuasion operates beneath our conscious recognition.

As recent studies have shown, AI can move people’s attitudes towards presidential candidates and policies by providing many factual claims that support their side.

In my view, protecting our personal agency requires an internal and external response.

Internally, we can defend civic agency by moving from a replacement mindset to a collaborative mindset: AI is not a substitute for the activities that define our human judgment — moral reasoning, critical reflection, and creative synthesis. Instead, AI should complement us in these endeavors. The output of a chatbot is not the final word but a starting point for discussion and critical inquiry. When used this way, AI can be a helpful tool for more and better civic engagement.

Externally, democratic societies need a robust regulatory framework designed to protect public discourse from covert manipulation. While autocratic regimes will try to compel AI companies to align outputs with their ideology, democracies must aim for AI to provide genuine choice rather than paternalistic steering. We require rigorous safety testing and independent benchmarks for cars, pharmaceuticals and financial products. AI demands equal oversight. Our goals should be transparency and the safeguarding of AI users’ cognitive independence.

AI can have a positive impact. When engineered to empower rather than to persuade, AI can strengthen personal autonomy and democratic participation. Instead of nudging our beliefs in a particular direction, AI systems can serve as tools to learn and inform. They can make complex topics more easily understandable, truly personalize learning, and dramatically extend our knowledge, productivity, and creativity. But realizing this potential requires a deliberate, collective effort across society.

Engineers and user interface designers can help by building models and interfaces that encourage dialogue rather than performative affirmation. Lawmakers and regulators can create and enforce transparency and outlaw state- or corporate-sponsored steering.

For us in higher education, it is our responsibility to prioritize AI literacy and stimulate independent thought. The ultimate challenge of the AI era may not be to create machines that can “think,” but rather to prevent ourselves from stopping to think.

Sebastian Zimmeck is an associate professor of computer science at Wesleyan University, where he directs the privacy-tech-lab .

articles.title: Trump spars with NBC reporter over Ramaswamy attack ad
articles.summary: President Trump engaged in a vigorous back-and-forth Friday with NBC reporter Monica Alba after tripling down on the Ohio governor’s race ad featuring Democratic nominee Amy Acton’s estranged mother calling her a liar. Reporters asked Trump about fellow Republicans denouncing the ad that was created by Vivek Ramaswamy, the GOP candidate for Ohio governor. “But…
articles.body:
President Trump engaged in a vigorous back-and-forth Friday with NBC reporter Monica Alba after tripling down on the Ohio governor’s race ad featuring Democratic nominee Amy Acton’s estranged mother calling her a liar.

Reporters asked Trump about fellow Republicans denouncing the ad that was created by Vivek Ramaswamy, the GOP candidate for Ohio governor.

“But they don’t know the facts,” Trump said. “Look … a mother is saying, ‘Don’t put my daughter there because she’s a terrible person and she’s a liar.’ Why shouldn’t somebody use that?”

Ramaswamy has confirmed his campaign funded the ad, which featured Acton’s mother, Donna Arthur, calling her a “liar” and insinuating that she has mental health issues. Acton has said she hasn’t spoken to her mother since she was a child and was sexually abused by her stepfather. Her mother stayed with the stepfather even after he was charged with sexually abusing Acton when she was 12, court documents show.

Alba pushed back at Trump’s response, asking, “Do the sexual abuse allegations mean nothing to you?”

Trump told her to slow down and asked what outlet she was with. He then went on to bash NBC News and called Alba a “fresh person” and a “horrible little reporter.”

“If my mother said bad things about me, do you think the Democrats would put it up? I think so. But my mother thought I was wonderful,” he said.

“This is a person, a mother, a smart woman — I watched, smart woman — she said her daughter is a disaster,” Trump continued. “Her daughter is a liar, and she felt that she had an obligation. And she also said her daughter lied about her opponent, which is Vivek Ramaswamy. If I had that ad, I should be so lucky to have an ad like that. Why wouldn’t you listen to a mother that says that? Why? Why would you … Miss NBC. Why wouldn’t you listen?”

Alba tried explaining to the president that Arthur stayed with the stepfather after he was charged, while Trump turned away from her and said, “I don’t know anything about a stepfather,” then, “You just keep talking.”

“I’m just answering you, sir,” Alba replied.

“I don’t know anything about stepfathers,” he repeated.

“A sad thing, and I feel like it was an exploitative thing to do. My mother is not well,” Acton told CBS affiliate WBNS .

Ramaswamy has argued the claims Arthur made about Acton are “not new.”

“Her mother has spoken out for years, and I don’t know Amy Acton’s mother and I’ve never met Amy Acton either. What I do know is that Amy Acton has been repeatedly and serially dishonest during this campaign,” Ramaswamy said.

Since the ad has aired, Acton is narrowly favored over Ramaswamy to win.

Decision Desk HQ, NewsNation ’s election partner, puts Acton’s chances of winning at 60 percent, compared with 40 percent for Ramaswamy, as of Wednesday. Last month, their chances were closer to 50-50.

articles.body:
It’s Friday , and it’s shaping up to be a busy one with lots of news breaking before lunchtime. Let’s dive in, shall we?

Programming note : Hello! We are Colin Meyn and Elliott Davis filling in for Cate. Please send your tips, comments and story ideas to cmeyn@thehill.com or edavis@thehill.com.

The president is campaigning in Fort Myers, Fla., this afternoon en route to the sunny environs of his Palm Beach resort.

It could be a gloomy stretch ahead with Democrats threatening to win races in historically red states. Trump rallied in Kansas and Iowa this week and added a stop in Mississippi next week — all states appear up for grabs 11 days out from Election Day.

He’ll rally today in Rep. Byron Donalds’s (R-Fla.) district, where Republican Jim Schwartzel is a heavy favorite against Democrat Victor Arias. Donalds is locked in a tough race for governor against Democrat David Jolly.

Democrats also see a slim chance of taking a Senate seat in Florida. Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) stumped with Angie Nixon in Tampa last week as she seeks to knock off Sen. Ashley Moody (R-Fla.), who was tapped to replace Marco Rubio when he became secretary of State.

Early voters: Before taking off for Florida, Trump told reporters that he and first lady Melania Trump would cast their ballots in Florida on Saturday.

He don’t stop: Trump will have about 24 hours to recharge at Mar-a-Lago before he’s back to the midterm grind.

He’s set to rally in Perry, Ga., on Saturday night; Port Huron, Mich., on Sunday afternoon; Corinth, Miss., on Monday; then Texas on Tuesday, with stops planned in Corpus Christi and Lubbock. He’ll hit Chillicothe, Ohio, on Wednesday.

Trump fielded questions from the press corps for about 15 minutes before taking off for Fort Myers around 11:30 a.m.

He denied reports that he told Elon Musk to restore full Starlink access to Ukraine, but he said he would if the issue wasn’t resolved. Ukraine says it’s still having trouble with the satellites when drones reach high speeds.

Trump also faced off with NBC News White House correspondent Monica Alba, who pressed him about his support for Vivek Ramaswamy’s attack ad featuring his opponent’s estranged mother. Worth a watch .

Some prominent Ohio Republicans are calling on their gubernatorial candidate to stop running the ad.

All eyes are on Musk after Politico reported Friday that Ukrainian interceptors still cannot use high-speed internet to shoot down Russian attack drones, potentially countering Trump’s message a day ago, when he said the SpaceX founder had lifted speed restrictions on his Starshield service.

The tech billionaire was under fire last week when his Starlink service cut off for objects that traveled more than 100 mph, impacting the capabilities of Ukraine’s drones, airplanes and helicopters. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky and Republican senators, such as Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.), called on Musk to explain what happened.

The Wall Street Journal reported Thursday that Trump called Musk and asked him to lift the slowdown of Starlink and Starshield, its military counterpart. But the president on Friday denied that. He added, however, that he will speak with Musk if the service is now fixed.

Meanwhile, Laura Loomer , a close ally and adviser to Trump, told The Hill’s broadcast partner NewsNation that the U.S. should keep helping Ukraine.

Zooming out: GOP lawmakers are now pushing for more congressional oversight on what some view as the Tesla CEO’s “space monopoly” out of fear that Musk will have too much power over future national security operations, The Hill’s Alexander Bolton reports .

The world’s richest person is making waves on the homefront, too. The Hill’s Julia Shapero reports that Musk has now spent more than $442 million in the midterm elections, including an influx of $76.8 million into his America PAC in the past month.

After saying earlier this year that he had gotten “a little too involved in politics,” Musk is back to spending loads of money to ensure Republicans keep control of Congress.

🏠 Trump added fuel to the fire late Thursday night by accusing Democratic Rep. Ilhan Omar (Minn.) of using a fake name amid a federal investigation into the progressive lawmaker’s immigration background. The president also called on Omar, whose Washington home was recently searched by federal investigators, to resign.

⚖️ While the Trump administration wants to get U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes off the case over the president’s proposed renovation of East Potomac Golf Links, an Insider analysis by The Hill’s Zach Schonfeld shows the district judge, an appointee of former President Biden, has not always ruled against Trump.

🗳️ Another reason for Democrats to be optimistic about taking control of the House after the midterms: Nonpartisan handicapper Cook Political Report shifted 19 seats in the party’s favor with 11 days until Election Day.

🎰 Casinos, tribes and unions: You might think these groups would be unlikely to work together, but The Hill’s Julia Shapero reports they’re doing just that when it comes to the fight on regulating prediction markets. Insiders can learn more here .

⛽ Oil prices are still elevated as the Iran war nears the eight-month mark. Futures for Brent crude, the international benchmark, were trading at $116 per barrel, while U.S. benchmark West Texas Intermediate traded at about $102. The prices are now at their highest point since May.

articles.title: Federal government stopped sharing information in Good, Pretti killings, Minnesota officials say
articles.summary: Minnesota officials said the Department of Justice (DOJ) has stopped sharing evidence related to the killings of Alex Pretti and Renee Good by immigration officers earlier this year. Minnesota officials said in a court filing reviewed by The Associated Press that the federal government stopped sharing evidence related to the two shooting deaths during President…
articles.body:
Minnesota officials said the Department of Justice (DOJ) has stopped sharing evidence related to the killings of Alex Pretti and Renee Good by immigration officers earlier this year.

Minnesota officials said in a court filing reviewed by The Associated Press that the federal government stopped sharing evidence related to the two shooting deaths during President Trump’s Operation Metro Surge in Minneapolis. Minnesota officials initially sued the DOJ for the evidence they said was needed to conduct an independent investigation of the shootings.

State officials have asked a judge to order the DOJ to hand over evidence they have on the shootings and said the federal government has no legal authority to obstruct their investigation. According to the filings, the DOJ agreed to share the evidence with state officials in July and began transferring materials to Minnesota but stopped the cooperation soon after.

Good, a mother of three, was shot and killed by an Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer through her car’s windshield after she attempted to drive forward after a heated interaction with an officer. After shooting through the windshield, the officer moved next to the driver’s side window and fired two more shots while standing an arm’s length away from Good.

Pretti, a nurse who was protesting the immigration enforcement operations, was killed weeks later after he approached officers while protesting and filming on his phone. Pretti was legally carrying a gun on his person, which was taken by an officer as a group of agents attempted to arrest him moments before shots were fired .

Hennepin County Attorney Mary Moriarty said in the filings that she was told on Sept. 10 that evidence sharing would be indefinitely on pause. In a DOJ reply earlier this week, the federal government argued that they have the power to decide what information they share with state authorities, The Associated Press reported.

Drew Evans, superintendent of the Minnesota Bureau of Criminal Apprehension, said in a legal declaration reviewed by The Associated Press that the DOJ has Good’s clothing and the cellphone of the officer who killed her. Evans also said the DOJ has not shared a recorded statement from the officer who killed Pretti, the guns used by officers on the scene or the gun taken from Pretti before he was shot.

articles.body:
In a televised presidential debate in Sao Paulo on October 18, Flavio Bolsonaro brought a number from Brazil’s prisons into an argument over crime. “Seventy-three percent”. The 45-year-old senator claimed that was the share of prisoners who had voted for his opponent, President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, 80. The figure came from polling stations inside detention facilities, where staff and eligible detainees awaiting trial could cast ballots. Convicted prisoners serving final sentences could not vote. Lula paused. “I want 100 percent,” he replied. “Even your father.”

Jair Bolsonaro, the absent father, had spent 28 years in Congress, where he repeatedly praised the 1964 military coup that ushered in more than two decades of dictatorship. He went on to become president, lost re-election to Lula in 2022 and was later convicted of plotting to overturn the result. He is serving a 27-year sentence under house arrest. A week after Lula’s inauguration, thousands of Bolsonaro supporters invaded and vandalised the presidential palace, Congress and Supreme Court in Brasilia, claiming without evidence that the election had been stolen.

Back in the studio, Flavio was promising to “redemocratise” Brazil. He demanded respect for the 56 million Brazilians who had voted for him and said he would send Lula into retirement.

On October 4, Brazil held the first round of its presidential election, alongside elections for the Chamber of Deputies and the Senate. Flavio received 56.1 million votes, or 47.03 percent of valid ballots, against Lula’s 53.9 million and 45.16 percent. Since then, Bolsonaro’s lead in the polls has narrowed, with several surveys placing the candidates within the margin of error. The latest readings suggest Lula is gaining ground, although just days before the October 25 run-off, it remains uncertain whether the president can overcome Flavio’s first-round lead.

The October 18 debate had begun with a discussion of armed groups spreading through Brazilian neighbourhoods. Nearly 69 million Brazilians say they perceive the presence of criminal gangs or militias in their neighbourhoods, even as the country’s murder rate falls. Flavio called for treating those organisations as narcoterrorists and for Brazil to join United States President Donald Trump’s Shield of the Americas alongside Javier Milei’s Argentina. He promised 500,000 additional prison places, easier civilian access to firearms and a reduction in the age of criminal responsibility from 18 to 16, and to 14 for certain serious crimes.

For residents of poorer neighbourhoods, Flavio proposed a Ministry of Prosperity, promising vocational training and credit to help families receiving government assistance to start businesses of their own. The word “prosperity” had a history of its own in Brazil’s influential evangelical churches, where sermons sometimes link material advancement to faith and individual endeavour.

Taken together, the promises linked the prospect of safer streets to a particular idea of prosperity, in which government assistance would become a starting point for vocational training, credit and small businesses.

Lula spoke of the social gains of his governments and of restoring democratic institutions after the Bolsonaro years. A former union leader who helped found the centre-left Workers’ Party (PT), he proposed stronger federal coordination of public security. The tougher approach to crime was not confined to Flavio’s campaign. Lula, too, supported lowering the age of criminal responsibility to 16 for certain serious offences.

Two days before the debate, Lula had stood among congressional leaders to celebrate a reform that would gradually bring Brazil’s six-day working week to an end, reducing hours from 44 to 40 without cutting wages. After initially criticising the reform as opportunistic, Senator Flavio Bolsonaro changed his position and voted for it, saying he had listened to workers on the campaign trail.

Lula had other economic gains to highlight. Unemployment in Brazil has fallen from 7.8 percent in 2023 to 5.3 percent this year, while real wages have risen. For many households, however, expensive credit and debt repayments have dampened the impact of any improvements. Flavio has sought to capitalise on the resulting economic frustration, as well as concerns about public security.

If re-elected, Lula would have to address those frustrations while dealing with a Congress reshaped by the October 4 legislative elections. In the 513-seat lower house, Bolsonaro’s Liberal Party (PL) won 121 seats, up from 97. The PT-led bloc moved from 82 to 88, while the largest alliance of traditional centre-right parties lost 18 seats. The sharpest rearrangement had taken place within the right, leaving the parliamentary left’s numbers largely intact.

The right’s gains raise a question about the kind of change the Bolsonaro movement represents. In an October Datafolha survey, 48 percent of Lula’s supporters mentioned social protection, while 41 percent of Flavio’s supporters expressed a desire for change. Yet the PL’s new deputies were hardly political novices. Of the 121 elected, 111 had held office before and 93 had belonged to other parties.

In 2002, the same party had placed Jose Alencar, a conservative textile magnate, next to Lula on the presidential ticket that first brought the former union leader to power. Alencar remained vice president until 2010, though he left the PL in 2005 amid a corruption scandal involving its leadership. Jair Bolsonaro joined only in 2021. The party now housed his family’s ambitions alongside politicians whose careers had begun under very different banners.

In a country where presidents rarely command a parliamentary majority of their own party, politicians of such experience are seldom without work. Governments change, and parties move between coalitions to negotiate cabinet appointments and influence over the funds that reach their constituencies. Established centre-right parties have served administrations of widely differing orientations. Jair Bolsonaro eventually relied on them after campaigning against the political establishment. His movement’s gains had not made those alliances obsolete.

Lula has spent much of his political career constructing governments with former adversaries. His current vice president and running mate, Geraldo Alckmin, once challenged him for the presidency as the candidate of the centre-right opposition. A fourth term would demand more of that experience, with the right holding greater power in Congress. Lula’s successor, Dilma Rousseff, was impeached in 2016 amid a deep recession and the collapse of her governing coalition, circumstances quite different from those Lula faces today.

The new balance of power would be particularly consequential for the Supreme Court. Alexandre de Moraes had overseen the case that sent Jair Bolsonaro to prison. As the Bolsonaro family accused him of political persecution, Lula’s party defended his authority as part of its defence of democracy. But the court has become a major target of the right’s parliamentary ambitions.

Moraes’s name had travelled through the October 4 Senate elections, in which 54 of the chamber’s 81 seats were contested. Candidates allied with the Bolsonaros promised to impeach him and curb the court’s powers. Some wanted its jurisdiction narrowed, while others sought to limit the authority of individual justices to act alone. The collapse of Banco Master, a private bank that had a lucrative contract with the law firm of Moraes’s wife, raised questions about possible conflicts of interest. The firm has denied wrongdoing.

A fourth Lula term would face 28 Liberal Party senators in an 81-seat chamber empowered to approve Supreme Court appointments and remove justices through impeachment. A survey by Folha de S. Paulo identified at least 49 members of the next Senate who had expressed support for impeaching Supreme Court justices in some circumstances. That was five short of the two-thirds required for removal, even before agreement on a particular case. Support for restricting the court’s powers extended beyond the Bolsonaro movement.

Congress’s growing power could also constrain Lula’s ability to deliver the economic and social improvements on which he has based much of his political appeal. Control over public money had been moving towards Congress. In 2025, parliamentary allocations for local projects reached about 47 billion reais ($9.3bn) in committed funds, more than four times their level 11 years earlier. Legislators increasingly choose where that money goes. A president can secure their votes for a particular measure without recovering control over the funds they distribute.

On Wednesday, Lula sent Congress a proposal to make public transport free on weekends and public holidays, allowing some workers who would soon have two days off to travel without paying fares. He suggested using money politicians had set aside for projects in their constituencies. The Speaker of the lower house welcomed the idea. He wanted the money to come from somewhere else.

The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

articles.title: Feds knocking on doors to question voters’ immigration status: CBS
articles.summary: We need to protect eligible Americans’ right to vote without fear. If the administration believes it can win voters over, the answer is policy and persuasion, not tactics that risk making people afraid to exercise their fundamental right.
articles.body:
We have officially moved into voter intimidation territory.

According to a new CBS News investigation, armed, uniformed Department of Homeland Security agents are going door to door in several states , questioning residents about their immigration status and whether they’ve registered to vote or cast ballots.

The administration says it’s targeting potential noncitizen voting. But noncitizens are already prohibited by law from voting in federal elections, and the evidence of widespread voter fraud simply isn’t there.

One Brennan Center study examining 23.5 million votes across 42 jurisdictions identified just 30 suspected cases of voter fraud . That’s roughly one for every million votes.

So why are federal agents knocking on people’s doors over an issue that the available evidence suggests is exceedingly rare?

A federal judge was likely confused as well, since they ruled Wednesday that these operations likely violate the Voting Rights Act and ordered restrictions on the practice in nine states under specified circumstances. The judge also warned of a high likelihood of error in the government’s process for identifying potential targets.

Let’s talk about all the errors that could be made here. A U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services whistleblower reported that employees were expected to review 40 people a day , spending roughly 12 minutes per person. How thoroughly can tens of thousands of records be vetted at that pace, particularly when American citizens are included in the data? Naturally, legal voters are going to get caught in the crossfire of this mess.

Rep. Bennie G. Thompson, the top Democrat on the House Homeland Security Committee, called the operation a “anti-democratic departure from the mission Congress set for the Department” and described it as a “law enforcement activity aimed at intimidating the public as the 2026 midterm elections are underway.”

I completely understand that concern. Imagine being a naturalized citizen, watching armed federal agents question your neighbors about voting. Even if you’re legally eligible to vote, you might wonder whether casting a ballot could put you or your family under scrutiny. That fear alone can keep people away from the polls.

And remember, former Trump adviser Steve Bannon said earlier this year : “You’re damn right we’re gonna have ICE surround the polls come November. We’re not gonna sit here and allow you to steal the country again.”

Sending ICE or any other armed federal agents to the polls is illegal, because federal law bans federal officers from interfering in elections. It’s also illegal because federal law bans troops and armed federal agents from being deployed anywhere an “election is held.”

Bannon’s rhetoric, combined with door-to-door investigations and recent scrutiny and investigations of voter-registration groups, is feeling like voter intimidation.

We’ve seen President Trump challenge the 2020 election results, including pressuring Georgia officials to “find votes.” Now, with the midterms approaching, voters are watching federal agencies expand their efforts to investigate alleged election fraud. Something we know is extremely rare. Claims of widespread voter fraud are unsupported by evidence and are being used to erode public confidence in elections.

We need to protect eligible Americans’ right to vote without fear. If the administration believes it can win voters over, the answer is policy and persuasion, not tactics that risk making people afraid to exercise their fundamental right.

Lindsey Granger is a NewsNation contributor and co-host of The Hill’s commentary show “Rising.” This column is an edited transcription of her on-air commentary.

articles.title: Reporter's Notebook: Congress braces for post-election game of musical chairs as leadership battles loom
articles.summary: Capitol Hill braces for leadership elections as Mike Johnson, Hakeem Jeffries, John Thune and Chuck Schumer all face uncertain futures ahead.
articles.body: Capitol Hill is about to embark on a biennial game of musical chairs. Everyone needs to find a seat when the music stops. Those who don’t are out. There are four sets of leadership elections pending in Congress over the next few weeks. House Republicans and Democrats will pick their top leaders. The same with Senate Republicans and Democrats. The entire House must elect a speaker when the new Congress convenes on Jan. 3. The full Senate chooses the majority leader. That’s decided individually by the majority party in the Senate. We anticipate a scramble for leadership positions in the days following the election, depending on which party captures the majority of each body for the new Congress. JORDAN EMERGES AS POTENTIAL NEXT GOP LEADER IF DEMS SEIZE HOUSE Let’s start with House Republicans. If Republicans maintain control of the House, the GOP will likely maintain its current leadership team of House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., Majority Leader Steve Scalise, R-La., and Majority Whip Tom Emmer, R-Minn. However, if the GOP loses control of the House, recriminations — and an epic game of vicious political musical chairs likely commences. The reason? In the minority, a party only has two top leadership positions compared to three in the majority. Will Johnson slide to minority leader? Does he want that slot? Does President Donald Trump want him in that position? Or someone else? Regardless, whoever Trump wants as the top House Republican is the one who gets that slot in the new Congress. Would Scalise become minority leader? Would he slide to minority whip? Where does Emmer fit in here? Could Emmer become the top House GOPer? Then there is Rep. Jim Jordan, R-Ohio. It’s clear that Jordan wants to become the top Republican in the House. He’s campaigned for Republican candidates and members for months and has raised money on the GOP’s behalf for years. It’s unclear if Jordan might be in a race against Johnson or any of the others soon. Keep in mind that Scalise, Emmer and Jordan all lost bids to become speaker when the House dismissed former House Speaker Kevin McCarthy, R-Calif., in the fall of 2023. In fact, Jordan lost multiple floor votes for speaker before the House Republican Conference nixed him as the GOP nominee. In the interim, Jordan has worked to build bridges among Republicans who opposed him three years ago. The Ohio Republican also remains a close ally of Trump. Jordan also maintains strong ties to the conservative House Freedom Caucus. JEFFRIES WELCOMES DEMOCRATIC SOCIALISTS INTO THE FOLD AS CRITICS WARN PARTY IS REVEALING 'EXACTLY WHO IT IS' The question is what rank-and-file Republicans want to do if they find themselves in the minority? Some might prefer a wholesale set of changes among the GOP leadership team. But it will come down to musical chairs. And somebody — if not several somebodies — probably lack a seat when the music stops. For the Democrats, their situation is easier. Let’s say Democrats do win control of the House. Yes, the Democratic Socialists of America and some possible members have reservations about promoting House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., to become speaker of the House. But it’s hard to see that Democrats wouldn’t tap him as the first Black speaker in American history. House Minority Whip Katherine Clark, D-Mass., would matriculate to majority leader. House Democratic Caucus Chairman Pete Aguilar, D-Calif., would likely become majority whip. However, if Democrats don’t win the House, would their top leaders remain in place? Unclear. Democrats have established high expectations. So one can envision a scenario where rank-and-file Democrats are so exercised about a midterm loss that they call for some new leaders if Democrats fail to flip the House in such a toxic political environment for Republicans. Then, there’s the Senate. Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., does not wield the same political currency with Trump as Johnson. The president has started to make demands of the Senate schedule or what he wants passed. The South Dakota Republican has resisted many of those entreaties. But what happens if Republicans lose control of the Senate? Many Senate Republicans are apoplectic at how the president treated Sen. John Cornyn, R-Texas, who formerly served as Senate GOP whip. They will rage if the president calls for the dismissal of Thune — in the minority but especially the majority. So far, Trump has kept things in check and not expressed direct displeasure with Thune personally. But one wonders how long that would continue. Especially considering what the president said about former Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell, R-Ky. – who ushered three Supreme Court nominees to confirmation under dramatic circumstances. THUNE MAKES BOLD PREDICTION ABOUT REPUBLICANS' SENATE CHANCES AS GOP PULLS MILLIONS FROM KEY RACES Who could step into a possible Senate GOP leadership void? Senate Majority Whip John Barrasso, R-Wyo., is the obvious choice. Barrasso appears closer to the president than Thune — and remains airtight when given the opportunity to criticize Trump. That could work in Barrasso’s favor if there’s an opening. But leadership elections are always about opportunities. And sometimes those figures with certain bona fides have too much baggage from being on the job for a while. Here are the names to watch if there’s a push for changes inside the GOP leadership ranks: Sens. Katie Britt, R-Ala., John Kennedy, R-La., and Rick Scott, R-Fla. A former Senate aide, Britt has a solid "inside game" and works well with the administration. Kennedy’s folksy manner makes him a darling of TV appearances. He also spent lots of time on the road campaigning for Senate Republican candidates. Scott ran for majority leader two years ago and lost to Thune and Cornyn in the first round. Then there are Senate Democrats. Some have lobbed gobs of criticism at Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y. His age. His style of politics seems archaic to some. But it’s hard to argue with success. Schumer likely becomes majority leader if Democrats flip the Senate. But things could change if Democrats fail to gain control of the body. Political observers don’t think Democrats have as good a chance at flipping the Senate as the House. So it’s not a done deal that Democrats will want new leadership if Democrats fail to gain control. The one "known" is the pending candidacy of Sen. Brian Schatz, D-Hawaii, to succeed retiring Senate Minority Whip Dick Durbin, D-Ill. However, one could envision a scenario where Schatz becomes the top Senate Democrat if Schumer departs. Like Britt, Schatz is an intense internal operator and understands the subtleties of the Democratic Caucus. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Others who may have an interest in a leadership post — if they don’t run for president — include Sens. Cory Booker, D-N.J., Chris Murphy, D-Conn., Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich., Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., and Chris Van Hollen, D-Md. Booker has credibility for his record-breaking 25-hour speech last year. Murphy appeals to the party as a telegenic spokesperson — and spoke on the floor for nearly 15 hours on gun violence in 2015. Slotkin is a moderate Democrat in a purple state who likes to tangle with the Trump administration — despite picking some of her spots to address the press corps. She’s said that the "old" Senate leadership models are no longer working. Warren commands the support of progressives. And Van Hollen already has the backing of Michigan Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed. This is a lot to sort out. And it all hinges on the election outcomes. Leadership elections usually take place in mid to late November. It’s possible there could be a delay in leadership elections if it takes a while to sort out which party controls which body of Congress. But the music is already playing. And everyone is jockeying for a seat because the music is about to stop.

articles.title: Trump administration sues to block Alaska Senate certification if Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan loses in November
articles.summary: The Justice Department is suing Alaska election officials to prevent them from certifying Senate race results if GOP Sen. Dan Sullivan loses next month.
articles.body: The Justice Department has filed suit against Alaska election officials, seeking to block the results of November’s U.S. Senate election from being certified unless incumbent Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan wins. In papers filed in federal court, attorneys for the DOJ argued the presence of Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. on the ballot could mislead supporters of the sitting senator, Daniel S. Sullivan. “For example, some supporters of Senator Sullivan likely will inadvertently vote for Daniel J. Sullivan,” the filing says. “To guard against this danger, it is vital that Defendants not certify any election result that may be impacted by voter confusion,” the suit says. The Trump administration is seeking a court order blocking the results from being certified “if: (1) Senator Sullivan does not win the election; and (2) had all votes cast for Daniel J. Sullivan been cast instead for Senator Sullivan and Alaska’s rank-choice process played out accordingly, Senator Sullivan would have won the election.” The filing by Associate Attorney General Stanley Woodward said the action was brought “to protect the integrity of the 2026 Senate election in Alaska.” The Trump administration filed the lawsuit Thursday, the same day Attorney General Todd Blanche told reporters that “it is not DOJ’s intention to, and it’s never our intention to, improperly interfere with elections or the state confirmation process or certification process.” “I’m not trying to not have an election certified. Of course not,” Blanche said, although there could be some “doomsday” scenario in which DOJ would seek to get involved. It’s unclear why the department decided to seek action now, with Election Day less than two weeks away. U.S. elections are run by state and local officials, who are charged with certifying results. The Justice Department’s role in U.S. elections is limited by law, which chiefly allows the department to safeguard civil rights and prosecute people who violate election law. While private citizens and candidates can sue to challenge ballots or election results, Justin Levitt, an NBC News contributor who was a Justice Department official during the Obama administration, said there’s no law that says DOJ can challenge ballots or delay certification. A DOJ spokesperson told NBC News in a statement that Sullivan’s “candidacy was intended to mislead voters and compromise the fairness of the ballot. Therefore, the Justice Department, consistent with the National Voter Registration Act enacted by Congress, is taking the necessary steps to ensure that this frivolous candidacy does not undermine the integrity of Alaska’s election or the will of its voters.” Sullivan Jr.’s candidacy has already been challenged in Alaska, where in August he finished in third place with 2.5% of the vote in the all-party primary. Democrat Mary Peltola received 49.5% and Sen. Sullivan received 41.4%. Sullivan Jr. was initially booted from the ballot in June after election officials found his candidacy was not in “good faith,” citing his choice to run using the name Dan instead of Daniel and being “affiliated with the Republican Party” when he had previously “never — according to the Division’s records — been affiliated with the Republican Party in Alaska.” The Alaska courts, however, ruled he could stay on the ballot. The November ballot does differentiate the two Sullivans. “Dan S. Sullivan” is listed with a “registered Republican” and “incumbent” next to his name, while the other is listed as “Daniel J. Sullivan Jr.” with no party affiliation next to his name. Sullivan Jr. did not respond to a request for comment on the lawsuit. Sullivan’s campaign and his Republican allies have charged Sullivan Jr. is a Democratic dupe, being used to draw votes away from the incumbent. President Donald Trump has repeatedly criticized Sullivan Jr. as a “cheat.” “It’s cheating. It’s a spoiler candidate to go on the ballot with the exact same name as your great Senator Dan Sullivan. This guy’s name is Dan Sullivan. He knew nothing about politics. He was just put there by the Democrats to confuse the voter, and it’s very unfair. But that’s what they do. They cheat. They lie. They steal,” Trump said in a video post on social media earlier this month. NBC News reported back in July that federal and state investigators were looking at whether Sullivan Jr. could be part of a conspiracy to confuse voters, citing two people with knowledge of the matter. The status of that investigation is unclear. A spokesperson for Peltola said earlier this year that her “campaign has no involvement with either Sullivan campaign.” Sullivan Jr., a former teacher, told The Associated Press back in June that his candidacy is no sham and that he’s not in cahoots with anybody. “I have every right to run for whatever office I’m qualified for, and I’m qualified for this office,” he said then. “I think I’m doing what most Americans would think would be a patriotic thing to do when you’re unsatisfied with the status quo. You stand up and say, ‘I’m going to fight for things I believe that are going to make my community better.’”

articles.title: Thune weighs nightmare scenario for GOP as Democrats threaten to flip House
articles.summary: John Thune told reporters he's confident Republicans can hold both chambers, but election forecasters see the House as a much tougher fight.
articles.body: FREMONT, Neb. — If Democrats are able to gain control of the House of Representatives, one relationship between the top two lawmakers on both sides of Congress could define the remainder of President Donald Trump's time in office. If that’s the outcome on Election Night, Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., would have to work with the Democratic leader who rises in the House, and that is expected to be House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., who has led Democrats in the lower chamber since 2023. But Thune, in an interview with Fox News Digital on the campaign trail in Nebraska, remained confident that wouldn’t be the outcome. THUNE MAKES BOLD PREDICTION ABOUT REPUBLICANS' SENATE CHANCES AS GOP PULLS MILLIONS FROM KEY RACES "Well, I mean, I think obviously that's an entirely different dynamic," Thune said. "You've got a situation with divided government and that creates a different incentive structure in terms of if you want to be able to get things done, but I don't assume for a minute that's going to happen." "I still think that when push comes to shove and people look at the choices in front of them that we have a really good shot at hanging on both the House and the Senate," he continued. Election forecasters predict that the Senate could stay in Republican control, though seven total races are considered toss-ups by the Cook Political Report. Republicans’ chances of holding onto power in the House, however, are murkier, given that dozens of battleground seats are in play that have shifted favorably toward Democrats. The GOP has had a grip on the lower chamber since 2022, when it flipped the House during former President Joe Biden’s presidency. But a deeply unpopular Trump, whose approval ratings have dipped to historic lows, and continued economic pressures could contribute to Democrats regaining power. JOHNSON DOWNPLAYS GOP'S MIDTERM WOES AS DEMOCRATS EYE HOUSE TAKEOVER: 'I AM VERY BULLISH' Jeffries’ office did not respond to an inquiry from Fox News Digital asking whether he could work with Thune if both won their respective leadership spots. There has been no love lost between the two men during this congressional term so far, with each sharply criticizing the other during key legislative fights. Thune blasted Jeffries and Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., earlier this year as talks began to break down over funding the Department of Homeland Security (DHS). The top Republican accused both of being "afraid of their shadows," and being controlled by their left flank. That prompted Jeffries to retort to reporters that it was Thune who was "scared of his own shadow" during the partisan standoff. During the 2025 government shutdown, Jeffries accused Thune of "trying to bluff his way into an agreement" on federal spending. Congress is no stranger to a divided government, either. From 2023 to early 2025, Republicans controlled the House and Democrats held a razor-thin majority in the Senate. SCHUMER WARNS OF REPUBLICAN ADVANTAGE THAT COULD CHANGE THE BATTLE FOR SENATE CONTROL During that time, according to data collected by the Pew Research Center, the split Congress produced 106 laws. This version of Congress has so far produced 121 laws, with some major legislative action happening, like the "big, beautiful bill" and a major housing affordability package, passing between historically long government shutdowns. Thune is laser-focused on keeping the GOP’s control of the Senate, which was under Democratic control until 2024, when Trump and Republicans clinched a trifecta in Washington, D.C. He’s crisscrossed the country for the last several weeks of the homestretch heading into the election on Nov. 3, boosting candidates in competitive races that could determine the balance of power in the Senate. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Republican control of the upper chamber, he contended, would be vital to continuing key chunks of Trump’s agenda, including confirming his judicial and other executive branch nominations. "So if you want to see the country succeed and move forward, we've got to have a majority in the U.S. Senate to work with this president," Thune said. "Hopefully with a majority in the House as well, but I am very committed to doing whatever I can in the next couple of weeks getting around the country on behalf of our candidates to ensure that we have that majority in the Senate."

articles.title: ‘Nobody knows the truth’: Akhilesh Yadav dismisses seat-sharing figures amid Congress's demand for 175-200 seats
articles.summary: LUCKNOW: Samajwadi Party chief Akhilesh Yadav on Friday dismissed speculation over the number of seats Congress has sought for the 2027 Uttar Pradesh
articles.body: LUCKNOW: Samajwadi Party chief Akhilesh Yadav on Friday dismissed speculation over the number of seats Congress has sought for the 2027 Uttar Pradesh assembly elections, asserting that nobody knows the actual seat-sharing formula being discussed between the two INDIA bloc partners.“Someone claims 172 seats and believes they have leaked the figure. Another says 160, while someone else claims 150. Everyone thinks they know the numbers, but nobody knows the truth. If we need to convince anyone to achieve that goal, we will do so. articles.title: Federal judge kicked off 'botch job' anti-DEI case after stunning appeals court rebuke
articles.summary: The Fifth Circuit called Judge Henry Wingate's handling of Mississippi's anti-DEI law challenge a "botch job" riddled with AI hallucinations and errors.
articles.body: A federal judge was removed from a challenge to Mississippi's anti-DEI law after the Fifth Circuit blasted his handling of the case as a "botch job," pointing to orders riddled with factual errors, an apparent AI-hallucinated case citation and faulty applications of Supreme Court precedent. In an opinion penned by Judge Jerry Smith, a Reagan appointee, the appeals court vacated Reagan-appointed Judge Henry Wingate's preliminary injunction blocking the law and ordered the case reassigned to a different judge — an "extraordinary" and "rarely invoked" move. "This district judge carelessly exercised his Article III power by issuing sloppy edicts based on falsehoods and fabrications," Smith wrote, adding that "the district court—or perhaps, being charitable, its AI agent—ignored and manipulated governing law, apparently to satisfy a policy agenda." The controversy surrounding Wingate’s handling of the case began with serious errors in a temporary restraining order he issued in July after a group of teachers, parents and students sued, arguing that a Mississippi state law restricting DEI-related practices in public schools and universities violated the First and Fourteenth Amendments. TRUMP ADMINISTRATION PROPOSES STRIPPING TAX-EXEMPT STATUS FROM SCHOOLS USING RACE-BASED PROGRAMS Wingate replaced the order just two days later after Mississippi officials flagged major factual errors, including 11 individuals and organizations identified as plaintiffs who were never a part of the case, two officials incorrectly named as defendants and unsupported claims that three schools had already canceled DEI programs because of the law. The original TRO also cited purported declarations from four people who did not appear anywhere in the record and "may not even exist," according to the Fifth Circuit. It also attributed language to the bill that does not appear in the law, including references to "race or sex stereotyping," "race or sex scapegoating," "critical race theory" and "institutional bias."
